title: The one division the crypt never makes

objectives.statement: Trace one chromosome pair through both meiotic divisions, naming which physical connection is undone at each division and what each product contains, contrast that with what a single mitotic division separates, and state how many functional gametes one meiosis yields in spermatogenesis and in oogenesis.

Compute the number of whole-chromosome combinations independent assortment alone can produce in one person's gametes and in the zygotes of a couple, compute crossovers per chromosome pair from measured genome-wide crossover totals, and state the assumption that any larger estimate of gamete diversity depends on.

Predict the products of a meiosis in which one chromosome pair fails to separate at division I versus at division II, state how many of the four products carry an abnormal chromosome number in each case and what the abnormal product contains, and apply centromere-marker reasoning to infer which division failed.

Separate the documented association between maternal age and aneuploidy from the mechanisms proposed to explain it, state for a cited study what its design can and cannot establish about mechanism, and identify statements that go further than the cited evidence supports.

Explain why a continuously renewing somatic tissue such as the colonic crypt runs no meiosis, using the difference between what a mitotic and a meiotic division separate, and contrast the role that new chromosome combinations play in the germ line with the role that new genetic differences play in a crypt.

scenes.title: A tissue that divides for a lifetime and never does this
scenes.contentHtml:
A tissue that divides for a lifetime and never does this

Somewhere in your descending colon, at the base of one of the tubes you have been reading about since lesson 01, twelve to sixteen stem cells are dividing. Each divides about once every twenty-four hours. Their daughters climb, differentiate on the way up, work at the surface for a few days, and are shed into the lumen. Much of the colonic lining renews on a three-to-five-day cycle, and the absorptive cells are replaced every four or five days.

One division a day, every day, for decades. Eighty years is about twenty-nine thousand days, so a single lineage at the crypt base runs of order tens of thousands of divisions.

Not one of them is a meiosis, which is the division this lesson is about.

That is worth sitting with, because meiosis is usually taught as though it were the interesting kind of cell division and mitosis the routine one. In your body the ratio runs the other way. Almost every division that has ever happened inside you has been the ordinary kind. Meiosis happens in one lineage only, and the colonic crypt is not it.

So this lesson opens with a question that comes before the mechanism: what job is meiosis doing that a crypt has no use for?

Two cells, and an arithmetic problem

Start from the thing meiosis exists to make possible.

A new human begins when two cells fuse. Those two cells are the gametes: a sperm cell from one parent and an egg cell from the other. The single cell that results from their fusion is the zygote, and every cell in the resulting body descends from it by ordinary division.

Now count chromosomes. An ordinary body cell carries 46 of them, arranged as 23 pairs. Suppose the sperm and the egg each carried 46 too. The zygote would carry 92. That person's own gametes would then carry 92, so their children would start from 184, and their grandchildren from 368. Three generations and the number has octupled.

So the gametes have to carry half. That much is obvious. What is not obvious, and what the rest of this lesson turns on, is that halving is a much harder operation than it sounds.

Halving does not mean discarding 23 chromosomes at random. A cell that kept both versions of chromosome 7 and no version of chromosome 12 would have 23 chromosomes and would be useless. What is needed is exactly one from each of the 23 pairs. Every pair contributes one member, and which member it contributes does not matter.

Read that requirement again and notice what it demands. The cell has to treat chromosome 7 from your mother and chromosome 7 from your father as a pair, and send one of them to each side. It has to sort partners.

Definition
id definition-homolog-and-ploidy

A homologous pair is the two versions of one chromosome that a person carries, one inherited from each parent. They are very similar in DNA sequence without being identical. Each member of the pair is a homolog, and the two homologs of a pair are partners rather than copies of each other.

A cell holding both members of every pair is diploid: 46 chromosomes in a human, as 23 pairs. A cell holding one member of every pair is haploid: 23 chromosomes. A gamete is haploid. The cell at the base of your crypt is diploid, and stays diploid every time it divides.

Ploidy counts chromosomes, and not copies of DNA. The distinction looks like pedantry here and turns out to be the whole of scene 2's argument.

That last sentence is the whole of the contrast, so here is the vocabulary for it. A somatic cell is any cell of the body that is not on the path to becoming a gamete. Your crypt cells are somatic. The lineage that does produce gametes is the germ line, and it is the only lineage in which meiosis happens.

What an ordinary division separates, and what it does not

An ordinary division cannot sort partners, and this is where the crypt makes the point for you.

Before any cell divides, its DNA is copied, so that each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined together. An ordinary division then pulls those sister chromatids apart, sending one to each daughter cell. Each daughter ends up with 46 chromosomes, exactly as the parent cell had.

During that division the maternal and paternal members of a pair are never brought together, never matched up, never treated as partners. They behave independently of one another. Each simply splits into its two sister chromatids.

That is exactly right for a crypt. A stem cell at the crypt base has to produce two cells carrying what it carried. Faithful copying is the entire requirement. A division that halved the chromosome number would leave 23 after one day and fewer than a dozen after two, and a lining whose cells were shedding chromosomes at that rate would not last the week.

Meiosis is the other kind of division. It is specialised for producing gametes, and in it the homologs of a pair are brought together and physically joined to each other before they are separated. Pairing partners is the operation an ordinary division never performs, and it is what makes halving possible instead of merely destructive.

Callout
id callout-two-prerequisite-gaps

Two things this lesson leans on belong to other lessons, and a reader who has done lessons 01 to 07 of this block will not have met either.

The ordinary division just described is mitosis, and the cell cycle it sits in, its checkpoints and its segregation machinery are the subject of PREM-05.08, the other lesson in this module about division. That lesson may not be available to you yet. So where this lesson needs a fact about mitosis it states the fact and cites its own source for it, and it keeps to the few facts the comparison actually needs.

Chromosomes themselves are the subject of PREM-06.02, "Chromosomes and genomes". What a chromosome is made of, how DNA is packed into one, and how a genome is organised across several of them are all owed to you there. This lesson defines the small amount of chromosome vocabulary its own reasoning needs, in the definition block above and in the glossary, and goes no further. If the word chromosome feels thin to you right now, that gap is the reason and it is not yours.

Where this lesson goes

Scene 2 works out why meiosis takes two divisions when one would seem to be enough, and which separation each one performs. Scene 3 makes you count the variation meiosis produces, because "enormous" is not a number and this one is computable. Scene 4 deals with a claim you will meet everywhere, that meiosis makes four gametes, which is true of one sex and false of the other. Scenes 5 and 6 take up what happens when a separation fails, which is where this material meets medicine. Scene 7 is practice, with the support falling away as you go, and it also carries the recovery routes for anything here that did not land. Scene 8 comes back to the crypt.

The human count of 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: a 2013 review of aneuploidy, which states it while defining its terms.

No source is cited for the statement that a crypt runs no meiosis, because it follows from the definitions above rather than from a measurement; the review of the colonic crypt used here mentions neither meiosis nor gametes anywhere.

scenes.title: One replication, two divisions, and the reason there are two
scenes.contentHtml:
One replication, two divisions, and the reason there are two

Take a single chromosome pair and follow it. Everything here happens to all 23 pairs at once, but one pair is enough to see the logic, and 23 copies of the same logic is all the rest amounts to.

Some vocabulary first, because the argument cannot be made without it and lessons 01 to 07 did not supply it.

Definition
id definition-machinery-vocabulary

The spindle is the apparatus of protein fibres a dividing cell builds to move chromosomes. It has two ends, called poles. Each chromosome is gripped at a single attachment point, a structure built on it that the spindle fibres catch hold of, and the spindle pulls each chromosome toward one pole or the other. Anaphase is the stage at which that pulling happens and the chromosomes actually move apart.

One division produces exactly two cells, and it is worth seeing why rather than accepting it. A division assembles one spindle; that spindle has two poles and no more; every chromosome is pulled to one pole or the other, so the contents end up gathered in two groups; and the cell then pinches into two between the groups. Two poles, two groups, two cells. A single division cannot make four.

Where a stage belongs to a particular meiotic division, a Roman numeral says which: anaphase I is the pulling stage of the first division and anaphase II the pulling stage of the second.

Callout
id callout-counting-convention

Three counts run through this scene and they do not move together. Watch all three.

When a chromosome is copied, the result is two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere, a constricted region where the joining and later the pulling both happen. That joined object still counts as one chromosome. Each chromatid is a complete copy of that chromosome's DNA.

So a human cell that has just replicated its DNA holds 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, and two DNA copies of every chromosome. Replication changed the second and third counts and left the first alone.

Ploidy counts chromosomes. Diploid is 46, haploid is 23, and a replicated chromosome counts as one either way.

What is there to separate

Before meiosis begins, the DNA is replicated. Your chromosome 7 from your mother is now two identical sister chromatids; your chromosome 7 from your father is now two identical sister chromatids.

Then the two homologs pair along their lengths. Each duplicated chromosome pairs with its duplicated homolog to form a bivalent, which contains four chromatids. How the two homologs locate each other among all the DNA in a nucleus is a real question and this lesson does not answer it.

So one pair, at the start of meiosis, is four chromatids in a single paired structure: four copies of that chromosome's DNA, two from the mother and two from the father.

Two things hold that structure together, and both need naming before the argument.

The exchange between homologs. Meiotic recombination is the process in which meiosis deliberately breaks its own DNA and repairs each break using the homolog as the template. Most breaks are repaired with no exchange of arms. Where a repair does end with the two homologs having swapped the segments beyond the break, the outcome is crossing over, and one such reciprocal exchange is a crossover.

A swap sounds like something that would let two chromosomes come apart, so be explicit about why it does the opposite. The exchange is physical. Afterwards the DNA of one homolog's chromatid runs continuously into what was the other homolog's chromatid; along that chromatid they have become one molecule with a join in it. The visible connection this produces is a chiasma, and the chiasmata created by crossing over hold the maternal and paternal homologs together until the spindle separates them at anaphase I.

The glue between sister chromatids. Cohesion is a protein glue holding sister chromatids together, running along the chromatid arms and also through the centromere. It is one substance in two locations, and the cell releases it in two stages. Where the two need distinguishing, this scene calls them arm cohesion and centromeric cohesion.

Why two divisions

Now the question in the scene title, and the answer is arithmetic before it is biology.

Stop at the end of the first division and look honestly at what you have. Each product holds 23 chromosomes, one from every pair. By the definition in scene 1 that is haploid: the chromosome number has been halved and one member of each pair is present. So why is meiosis not finished here?

Because the chromosome number is not the only thing that has to be halved.

Each of those 23 chromosomes still consists of two chromatids, and each chromatid is a complete copy of that chromosome's DNA. The cell holds 23 chromosomes and two DNA copies of every one of them. A gamete has to carry one copy of each chromosome, because fusion has to produce a cell with two copies and no more, one from each parent. A cell handing on two copies of its own chromosome 7 would be passing on both of the copies it made, and the child would receive two versions of that chromosome from one parent instead of one.

So there are two different halvings to perform, and they are halvings of different things.

  • The first division halves the chromosome number, 46 to 23, by separating partners.
  • The second division halves the number of DNA copies per chromosome, two to one, by separating copies.

Neither division can do the other's job, because they act on different pairings. That is the reason there are two.

The count for the single pair you are following makes the same point in one line. The bivalent holds four chromatids, so four copies of that chromosome's DNA. A gamete needs one. Each division halves. Four to two to one is two halvings, so two divisions, and since each division doubles the cell count the products go one cell to two to four.

Callout
id callout-what-the-counting-does-not-settle

The argument above takes replication as given, and replication before meiosis is an observed fact: meiosis is a single phase of DNA replication followed by two cell divisions. Given the replication, two divisions follow from the counting.

What the counting does not explain is why meiosis replicates first at all. A cell that skipped replication would hold 46 chromosomes of one chromatid each, and a single division could in principle halve that to 23. Why the process instead copies everything and then divides twice is a question about how meiosis is coupled to the cell cycle and how it evolved, and this lesson does not answer it.

Which separation happens first, and why the order is fixed

Counting says there are two divisions. It does not say which separation each one performs, and that is the second question. The staging of cohesion release settles it.

At the start of anaphase I, the cohesion along the chromatid arms is degraded. The arms come unglued, the chiasma no longer holds the pair, and the two duplicated homologs move to opposite poles.

Count all three numbers. Each product now holds 23 chromosomes instead of 46, one from each pair. Each of those 23 is still two chromatids joined at the centromere, because the cohesion at the centromere was untouched. So the chromosome count per cell fell from 46 to 23, the chromatid count per cell fell from 92 to 46, and the number of DNA copies per chromosome is still two.

At the second division, the centromeric cohesion is degraded, held until then by cohesins specific to meiosis. Only now do the two sister chromatids of each chromosome come apart.

Count again. Each product holds 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid, and one DNA copy per chromosome. That is a gamete.

So the first division separates partners and the second separates copies, and the ordering exists because arm cohesion goes first while centromeric cohesion is protected. Reverse the staging and the first division would pull sister chromatids apart while the homologs were still paired, which would sort no partners at all.

The vocabulary follows the arithmetic. The first division is reductional, because the chromosome number falls. The second is equational, because it does not.

How the cell makes the first division grip differently

A fair objection: if the spindle machinery is much the same in both divisions, what stops the first division from simply pulling sister chromatids apart?

Part of the answer is the cohesion staging already described. The other part is geometry at the attachment point.

In mitosis, the attachment points of two sister chromatids face in opposite directions, back to back. Fibres from opposite poles catch them and the sisters are pulled apart. That arrangement is called bi-orientation, and it is why mitosis separates copies.

At the first meiotic division the arrangement is changed. The attachment points on one homolog's two sister chromatids are turned to face the same way, side by side, so that both are caught by fibres from the same pole. The two sisters are pulled as a unit, and what gets pulled apart is the pair of homologs. This side-by-side arrangement is what establishes a reductional division. At the second division the geometry reverts to back to back, which is why the second division separates sisters after all.

Callout
id callout-mono-orientation-scope

A bound on that last paragraph. Which proteins hold the two attachment points side by side has been worked out mainly in yeast. The geometric contrast itself, side by side at the first meiotic division against back to back in mitosis, is the part this lesson uses.

One event, two jobs

Notice what has quietly happened to crossing over.

Crossing over is normally introduced as the mechanism that generates variety, and scene 3 counts how much. In this scene it turned up doing something else: making the chiasma that holds a pair together until the first division pulls it apart. One event, two jobs.

That has a consequence you can predict before anyone tells you. A pair of homologs that made no crossover has no chiasma, and nothing is holding it together. In mutant organisms with a reduced frequency of crossing over, some chromosome pairs do lack chiasmata; those pairs fail to segregate normally, and many of the resulting gametes end up with too many or too few chromosomes.

That is not confined to laboratory mutants. It happens in humans without any mutation at all: over 10 per cent of human oocytes contain at least one bivalent with no crossover, and scene 6 takes up what follows from that.

Hold on to it, because it is the hinge between the two halves of this lesson. The event that creates variation is the same event whose absence causes a specific failure.

Check
id check-what-separates-when

Answer from memory, then check against the two counting passages above.

  1. A human cell has just replicated its DNA before meiosis. How many chromosomes does it hold, how many chromatids, and how many DNA copies of each chromosome?
  2. At the end of the first division, is the cell haploid? Give the chromosome number, and say what is still doubled.
  3. So what is the second division for? Name the quantity it halves.
  4. How many cells exist after the first division, and how many after the second? Why can one division not produce four?
  5. Two things give way at anaphase I: name both, and name the one thing held back until the second division.
  6. Why would reversing the staging of cohesion release stop meiosis from sorting anything?

A cell-biology textbook chapter on meiosis supplies the single round of replication followed by two divisions, the bivalent and its four chromatids, the separation of duplicated homologs at anaphase I and of sister chromatids at anaphase II, the degradation of arm cohesins at the start of anaphase I against the meiosis-specific centromeric cohesins degraded at the second division, the reciprocal exchange of segments between homologs, the mechanical role of chiasmata in holding homologs together until anaphase I, and the consequence in mutant organisms when a pair lacks a chiasma. The figure of over 10 per cent of human oocytes carrying at least one crossover-less bivalent comes from a 2012 review of human aneuploidy, and appears here so that the mutant-organism finding is not left looking irrelevant to people.

The reading that cutting arm cohesion is what releases the chiasma is this lesson's inference from two statements that sit adjacent in that chapter, and not a mechanism any source states.

The attachment-point geometry, back to back in mitosis against side by side at the first meiotic division, and the statement that this arrangement establishes a reductional division, come from a 2021 review comparing mitosis and meiosis. That review's molecular account of which proteins impose the side-by-side arrangement rests largely on work in fission yeast, which is why the callout bounds it. The same review supplies the separation of sister chromatids in mitosis. The 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs come from a 2013 review of aneuploidy.

The three-count bookkeeping, the argument that the two divisions perform two different halvings, the derivation that one spindle with two poles yields two cells, and the observation that reversing the cohesion staging would sort nothing are this lesson's own way of organising sourced facts.

scenes.title: Count it: how many different gametes can one person make?
scenes.contentHtml:
Count it: how many different gametes can one person make?

"Meiosis generates enormous genetic variation" is the sentence every course uses, and it teaches nothing, because enormous is not a quantity. Some of this variation is exactly countable, some is measurable, and some cannot honestly be reduced to a single number at all. This scene does all three and says which is which.

Step 1: assortment alone, and exactly what it counts

Go back to the first division. Each of the 23 bivalents lines up and its two homologs are pulled to opposite poles. Which pole receives the maternal homolog is settled independently for every pair: chromosome 1 going one way tells you nothing about which way chromosome 2 goes.

That is independent assortment: a binary choice repeated 23 times.

Worked Example
id worked-example-counting-combinations

One gamete, counting the parental origin of whole chromosomes.

Pair 1 sends either its maternal or its paternal homolog into this gamete: 2 ways. Pair 2 does the same, independently, so two pairs give 2×2=42 \times 2 = 4 ways. Three pairs give 8. The pattern is 2 multiplied by itself once per pair, so 23 pairs give 2232^{23}.

Working it out: 210=10242^{10} = 1024, so 220=10242=10485762^{20} = 1024^2 = 1\,048\,576, and 223=220×8=83886082^{23} = 2^{20} \times 8 = 8\,388\,608.

Textbook treatments give the same figure: from this process alone an individual could in principle produce 2 to the power n genetically different gametes, where n is the number of pairs, which for a human is 23. The exponent is the count of pairs and never the count of chromosomes, and the two differ by a factor of two. The phrase "at least" that the textbooks attach to this figure is doing real work: it is a floor, because assortment is only one of the two mechanisms, and the next steps add the other.

Be precise about what those 8.4 million combinations are combinations of. Crossing over rearranges chromosome arms, so the chromosome you pass on may be maternal along part of its length and paternal along the rest. What a reciprocal exchange does not do is move a centromere from one homolog to the other: the exchange swaps the material beyond the break, and each chromatid keeps its own centromere. So the exact thing 2232^{23} counts is the number of distinct patterns of parental origin across the 23 centromeres, which is precisely the thing the first division sorts.

Hold that. Scene 5 needs it, and it is why the marker used there has to sit at a centromere.

Now a couple. A zygote takes one gamete from each parent, and those two choices are independent of each other:

Seven times ten to the thirteen distinct centromere-origin patterns, from assortment alone.

Stop on that, because you have met a number like it. Lesson 01 put the number of cells in an adult human body at the order of ten to the thirteen, around three times ten to the thirteen for a 70 kg reference man. Divide: 7.04×10137.04 \times 10^{13} over 3×10133 \times 10^{13} is about 2.3. The count of chromosomally distinct children one couple could produce, ignoring crossing over entirely, is a little over twice the number of cells in a body. Lesson 01 also quoted a second, larger estimate of the body's cell count, so treat the comparison as an order-of-magnitude match and not as a fixed ratio.

Step 2: how much crossing over actually happens

Crossing over is the second mechanism, and unlike the first it has to be measured. It has been.

The measurement works by staining cells caught in the act of meiosis for a protein that gathers at crossover sites, then counting the bright spots, called foci, in each cell. Each focus marks one crossover.

The cells come from the two tissues where meiosis happens. A spermatocyte is a cell part-way through meiosis in the testis; an oocyte is a cell part-way through meiosis in the ovary. In one study, the counts were 49.09 foci per cell in males, across 4660 spermatocytes from 56 testicular biopsy samples, and 69.25 per cell in females, across 2038 oocytes from fetal ovarian tissue from 63 donors. The standard errors, which say how tightly each mean is pinned down by that many cells, were 0.07 and 0.29 respectively: both means are precise.

Roughly 49 crossovers per meiosis in the male and 69 in the female, genome-wide. Divide by the number of pairs:

About two crossovers per chromosome pair in the male and about three in the female.

Step 3: a prediction from that average, and the measurement that refuses it

Here the arithmetic invites a conclusion, and it is worth following it into the wall.

Scene 2 established that a bivalent with no crossover has no chiasma and nothing holding it together. At an average of two or three crossovers per pair, you would expect almost every pair to receive at least one, and you would expect the sex with more crossovers to have fewer empty pairs.

The measured frequency of bivalents with no crossover focus was 0.38 per cent in males and 2.60 per cent in females.

Rare in both, so the first half of the prediction holds. But the second half is backwards. The female has about 40 per cent more crossovers per meiosis and about seven times as many bivalents with none.

An average cannot explain that, and the reason is that an average is not a distribution. A second study measured the spread: the cell-to-cell variation in crossover number, expressed as a percentage of the mean, was 18 per cent in females against 10 per cent in males. The female process is nearly twice as variable between cells. A higher mean with a much wider spread can easily leave more cells and more individual bivalents at zero.

That same study found something sharper. Meiosis marks out more sites as candidate crossovers than it finishes. In human female meiosis about a quarter of the sites committed to becoming crossovers never complete the process, while in the male essentially all of them do. So the female is both less consistent and less efficient at finishing what it started, and either finding alone would help explain the empty bivalents that the mean does not.

Two lessons from this step. A mean and a rate of failure are different questions, and an average will mislead you about the tails. And a prediction that fails against data is more informative than one that succeeds, provided you look at why.

Step 4: checking a number against itself

Genetic distances are quoted in centimorgans, a unit of how often two positions on a chromosome are separated by crossing over, and not a unit of physical distance. A single crossover in a meiosis separates the positions on either side of it in half the resulting gametes, and 50 per cent recombination is defined as 50 cM, so one crossover contributes about 50 cM to a map. The focus counts therefore predict total map lengths of

and those are exactly the genome-wide genetic lengths the same study reports: 2455 cM in males and 3463 cM in females.

Which teaches something about reading a paper, and confirms nothing. The agreement is perfect because the authors calculated those map lengths from the focus counts using the conversion just applied. Two numbers that agree to four figures were never independent measurements. The same authors note that linkage studies, which measure map length by tracking inheritance through families and so arrive at it a genuinely different way, report longer maps than these. Two different methods disagreeing is information. One measurement restated in other units is not.

Step 5: what crossing over does to the count, and what it does not

Now the tempting calculation, and why this lesson will not give you a headline number for it.

The tempting version runs: assortment gave 23 binary choices, and crossing over adds 49 more switch points, so the count becomes 223+49=272≈4.7×10212^{23+49} = 2^{72} \approx 4.7 \times 10^{21}.

That figure is wrong, and it is worth taking apart because every one of its four faults is a real property of meiosis.

  1. A crossover touches two chromatids, not four. The 49 is a count per meiosis, and a bivalent holds four chromatids while a gamete receives one. Any single crossover has about an even chance of landing on the chromatid that ends up in a given gamete. So a gamete does not carry 49 switch points.
  2. The positions are not fixed slots. Crossover sites differ from one meiosis to the next, so there is no standing set of 49 independent segments to choose from.
  3. Crossovers are not placed independently of each other. One crossover reduces the chance of another nearby.
  4. Nearby segments are not free choices. Two positions close together on one chromosome travel together far more often than not.

Objection 1 is the only one that can be corrected by arithmetic, so correct it. If each of about 49 crossovers has an even chance of being on the inherited chromatid, a gamete carries about 24 switch points, spread over 23 chromosomes: roughly one per chromosome. That is a defensible and useful figure. The typical chromosome you pass on is not either of the two you received; it is one of them with about one join in it.

Push that back into a count and you would get something like 223+24=247≈1.4×10142^{23+24} = 2^{47} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{14}. That is larger than assortment alone by a factor of 2242^{24}, which is about 17 million. Objections 2 to 4 still apply to it, so treat it as an upper bound with its assumption named and not as a result.

Callout
id callout-what-to-quote

What to quote from this scene, and how.

Quote 8.4 million as a count, because it is one: an exact count of centromere-origin patterns for one person's gametes. Quote about 24 switch points per gamete, or about one per chromosome, as an estimate with a stated assumption. Quote the effect of crossing over on the total as an increase of many orders of magnitude, and give a figure only alongside the assumption it rests on. Do not quote 2722^{72} at all.

Where the crossovers come from

One more measurement, because it changes what you think crossing over is.

Scene 2 said meiotic recombination begins by breaking the cell's own DNA. Those breaks can be counted the same way, by staining for a protein that gathers at them. In the same study, the count averaged 134.07 per cell in males, from 44 spermatocytes, and 250.28 per cell in females, from 39 oocytes.

So roughly 134 breaks yield about 49 crossovers in the male, and roughly 250 breaks yield about 69 in the female. Most breaks are repaired without producing a crossover at all. Meiosis makes far more damage than it converts into exchanges.

The second study puts the break counts higher, at around 200 per nucleus in males and around 400 in females. Against the first study's figures that is about 50 per cent more in males and about 60 per cent more in females. Two counts of the same quantity differing by that much, in the same direction for both sexes, is worth reporting as a disagreement instead of averaging away. What both agree on is the sex difference and the large excess of breaks over crossovers.

Check
id check-count-the-variation
  1. Compute 2 to the power 23. State exactly what that number counts, and name the one feature of a chromosome whose parental origin it tracks.
  2. A friend says crossing over multiplies the number of possible gametes by about 49. Give two separate reasons that is wrong, one about the arithmetic and one about the biology.

scenes.title: Four products, and the meiosis that keeps only one
scenes.contentHtml:
Four products, and the meiosis that keeps only one

Almost every account of meiosis you will read says it produces four gametes from one cell. Two divisions, one cell becoming two becoming four, each haploid. The arithmetic is clean and the diagram is easy to draw.

It is also only half true, and the half that is false is the half that matters for the rest of this lesson.

The two processes need names. Spermatogenesis is the production of sperm cells, which happens in the testis. Oogenesis is the production of egg cells, which happens in the ovary. Both run meiosis. They run it very differently.

Misconception
id misconception-four-gametes

The claim. One meiosis produces four gametes.

Where it holds. In spermatogenesis it is accurate. Both divisions are symmetrical, the cytoplasm is split roughly evenly each time, and four viable gametes result from one starting cell.

Where it fails. In oogenesis both divisions are deliberately lopsided. The first division produces one large cell and a much smaller first polar body. The second division produces the egg and a second polar body. Half the genome is segregated into the polar bodies, and only a single viable gamete comes out of the whole process.

Why the error is not harmless. Four equal products and one product plus discards are different processes with different failure behaviour. A cell that is going to keep only one of its four chromosome sets, and that has been holding those chromosomes in a paused state for decades, is running under constraints that a symmetrical division does not face. Scene 6 is about what those constraints do, and the four-gamete picture hides all of it.

The corrective test. Ask how many functional gametes come from one meiosis and in which sex. If the answer is "four" without a qualifier, the answer is describing spermatogenesis and calling it meiosis.

A note on how many polar bodies

You may meet the figure of three polar bodies instead of two, on the reasoning that four products minus one egg leaves three. Both figures are in circulation, and the count is two or three depending on whether the first polar body goes on to divide again. This lesson says two, which is what the source it follows describes.

The number that carries the teaching is not two or three. It is one: one functional gamete per meiosis in the female, against four in the male.

The other asymmetry, which is time

The second difference between the two processes is more extreme than the first, and it is easy to miss because it is not visible in any diagram of chromosomes.

Spermatogenesis runs throughout life. It starts and it continues, producing cells continuously.

Oogenesis does not work like that at all. Oocytes are formed in the ovary during fetal development, before birth. They enter meiosis and then stop, arrested in late prophase of the first division. Prophase is the long preparatory stage of any division, the part where chromosomes condense and, in meiosis, where homologs pair and cross over; it comes well before the anaphase pulling scene 2 described. Oocytes are maintained in that arrested state for decades. A cell that completes its first meiotic division in a woman of thirty-five started that division roughly thirty-five years earlier and spent the interval paused partway through it.

Then, after the first division finally completes, the cell arrests a second time, at metaphase of the second division. Metaphase is the stage at which the chromosomes have finished lining up on the spindle and are ready to be pulled, so the cell is poised one step short of anaphase. It waits there. Fertilisation is the event that triggers completion of the second division.

So the two divisions of one female meiosis can be separated by decades from its own beginning, and the second division does not finish unless a sperm arrives.

Checkpoints, and a difference in stringency

One further contrast belongs here, because scene 6 needs it.

Cells have surveillance mechanisms that hold a division until the chromosomes are properly attached to the spindle. In oocytes, during the first meiotic division, that surveillance appears weak and ineffective at detecting misalignment compared with its performance in mitosis. Looking across the two sexes, the checkpoints operating during spermatogenesis are described as stringent enough that errors are extremely rare, while the checkpoint response to errors during oogenesis is described as poor.

Put the three asymmetries side by side and a pattern appears that you can reason from instead of memorising.

Spermatogenesis Oogenesis
Functional gametes per meiosis four one
When it happens throughout life begins before birth, then arrests for decades
Checkpoint response to error stringent; errors extremely rare poor
Crossovers per meiosis (scene 3) about 49 about 69
Bivalents with no crossover marker 0.38% 2.60%

Read the rows carefully, because they do not all do the same work.

Three of them predict more segregation errors in the female: the decades of arrest, the poor checkpoint response, and the seven-times-higher rate of bivalents with no crossover marker. Those three point the same way, and if you were asked to predict which sex misses more chromosomes before seeing any data, those are the rows that would tell you.

One row makes no prediction at all. Four functional gametes against one is a difference in yield, and nothing about yield says anything about how often a chromosome goes to the wrong pole.

And one row points the other way. More crossovers per meiosis should mean fewer pairs left without a chiasma, so the female's 69 against the male's 49 predicts that the female should do better. She does worse, by a factor of about seven, and that is exactly the failed prediction scene 3 spent a step on: an average does not fix a failure rate, and the resolution was in the spread and in the proportion of crossovers that never finish.

So the table is a genuine forecast from three rows, a silence from one, and a warning from one.

Callout
id callout-boundary-reproductive-material

This scene and the two after it are a teaching example, not medical advice: they describe reproductive and prenatal biology using published population figures, and contain no screening test, threshold, age recommendation, individual risk figure or reproductive decision.

Check
id check-asymmetries

  2. Roughly how long can a human oocyte spend arrested partway through its first meiotic division?
  3. What event releases the second arrest?
  4. Of the five rows in the table, three predict that one sex will make more segregation errors. Name those three, and name the sex.
  5. One row makes no prediction about error rates at all. Which, and why not?
  6. One row predicts the opposite of what is observed. Name it, and say which earlier scene explains why the prediction fails.

scenes.title: Which division failed, and how anyone could tell
scenes.contentHtml:
Which division failed, and how anyone could tell

Everything so far has assumed the separations work. Occasionally during meiosis chromosomes fail to separate normally into the four haploid products, and that failure has a name: non-disjunction. Some of the products end up lacking a chromosome and others end up with more than one copy.

Now, scene 2 established that the two divisions separate different things. So a failure at the first division and a failure at the second should not produce the same wreckage. Work out what each produces, and you will find they differ in two ways that anyone can check.

Setting up the notation

Follow chromosome 21 through a single meiosis, in spermatogenesis, so that all four products survive and can be counted. Take one pair:

  • M is the homolog inherited from the mother. Replication has made it two sister chromatids, M₁ and M₂, which are identical to each other.
  • P is the homolog inherited from the father, replicated into P₁ and P₂, identical to each other.

M and P are similar in sequence without being identical, because they came from different people. M₁ and M₂ are identical, because one was copied from the other. That distinction is the whole of what follows.

A normal meiosis gives four products: M₁, M₂, P₁, P₂. Each carries exactly one chromosome 21.

Case A: the first division fails

The first division is supposed to send M one way and P the other. Suppose it does not, and both go to the same side.

One cell receives all four chromatids, M₁ M₂ P₁ P₂, which is two chromosomes. The other cell receives no chromosome 21 at all.

The second division now proceeds normally in both. In the first cell, sisters separate: one product gets M₁ and P₁, the other gets M₂ and P₂. Which maternal chromatid travels with which paternal one is arbitrary and makes no difference to anything below; what is fixed is that each product receives one maternal-derived and one paternal-derived chromatid, because M and P split independently of each other. Each of those products therefore carries two chromosome 21s. In the second cell there is nothing to separate, so both of its products carry none.

Worked Example
id worked-example-first-division-failure

Products of a first-division failure, one pair affected:

Product Chromosome 21 content Count
1 M₁ and P₁ 2
2 M₂ and P₂ 2
3 none 0
4 none 0

Four of four products are abnormal. Two carry an extra copy and two carry none.

And note what the two-copy products carry: one maternal homolog and one paternal homolog. Two chromosomes that are not identical to each other.

Case B: the second division fails

Now let the first division work correctly. M goes one way, P the other. One cell holds M₁ M₂, the other holds P₁ P₂.

At the second division, suppose the sisters fail to separate in the cell holding M. Both M₁ and M₂ go into one product; the other product from that cell gets nothing. The cell holding P divides normally and gives two ordinary products.

Worked Example
id worked-example-second-division-failure

Products of a second-division failure, one pair affected:

Product Chromosome 21 content Count
1 M₁ and M₂ 2
2 none 0
3 P₁ 1
4 P₂ 1

Two of four products are abnormal. One carries an extra copy, one carries none, and two are entirely normal.

And what the two-copy product carries: M₁ and M₂, which are copies of the same homolog. Two chromosomes that are identical to each other.

The two differences, stated plainly

Put the cases side by side.

First division fails Second division fails
Products with wrong copy number 4 of 4 2 of 4
Normal products none two
The extra-copy product contains two different homologs two copies of one homolog

The first row is a difference in how much of the output is spoiled. The second row is the interesting one, because it survives into the resulting person and can be read years later.

Reading it backwards from a marker

If a product carrying two copies fuses with a normal gamete, the result carries three copies of that chromosome: a trisomy, written 2N+1. If a product carrying none fuses with a normal gamete, the result carries one: a monosomy, written 2N-1.

Both are cases of aneuploidy, which is the word this lesson's outcome turns on: an unbalanced chromosome number, in which certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs. A balanced number is called euploid, and for a human that is 46 in 23 pairs. Trisomy and monosomy are whole-chromosome changes, as distinct from segmental changes in which only pieces of chromosomes are gained or lost; this lesson deals only with whole chromosomes.

Two words are needed for this, and neither has appeared in this block before.

Definition
id definition-heterozygous-homozygous

Pick one position on a chromosome and read the DNA sequence there on each copy a cell holds. If the copies read differently, the cell is heterozygous at that position. If they read the same, it is homozygous there.

The words describe the comparison at one position, and nothing else. They say nothing about the whole chromosome and nothing about any trait.

Now a shift of generation to keep track of. Up to this point M and P have been the two homologs of the person whose meiosis you were following. From here the question is asked about a child, so the person making the gamete is that child's parent, and it is the parent's two homologs that M and P name.

Suppose you have a trisomic individual and both parents available, and you can read DNA sequence differences at the centromere of the tripled chromosome. What do you see?

  • If the error was at the first division, the two copies from the contributing parent are different homologs, so they carry different sequence at the centromere. The individual is heterozygous there for that parent's two versions.
  • If the error was at the second division, the two copies from that parent are copies of one homolog, so they carry the same sequence. The individual is homozygous there.

That is exactly the method used. Studies of the origin of naturally occurring trisomies use centromeric heterozygosity or homozygosity to infer the meiotic stage at which the error occurred. The reasoning you just did is the reasoning the method rests on.

Work out for yourself why the marker has to sit at the centromere and not elsewhere along the chromosome. Scene 3 gives you what you need: crossing over swaps segments between the two homologs along their lengths. A marker some distance from the centromere may therefore have been exchanged, so its sequence no longer tells you which homolog the centromere came from. The centromere is the part whose parental identity the first division actually sorts.

What the method has found

Applied to 170 infants with trisomy 21 in one population-based study, the distribution of origin was 86 per cent maternal, and within those, 75 per cent at the first division and 25 per cent at the second. Nine per cent were paternal, split evenly between the two divisions. Five per cent arose not in meiosis at all but by a mitotic error after fertilisation.

Two things in that result are worth pausing on. The overwhelming maternal excess is what scene 4's table predicted. And the presence of a mitotic category is a reminder that "trisomy" names an outcome and not a mechanism.

Two boundaries on the model you have just built

The clean two-case analysis above is a model, and two of its edges need marking.

It counted four products. That is spermatogenesis. In oogenesis, as scene 4 established, only one of the four becomes the egg and the rest are polar bodies. The "four of four" and "two of four" rows still describe what the divisions did, but whether the error is transmitted depends on which product is kept.

Human oocytes do more than these two things. A study of 218 oocytes from donors aged 9 to 43 classified errors into three patterns, and only one of them is first-division non-disjunction as modelled above. The others are precocious separation of sister chromatids, in which the sisters of one homolog separate already at the first division, and reverse segregation, in which both homologs split their sister chromatids at the first division. Sisters separating at the first division is not a possibility the two-case model contains at all.

So treat the two cases as a tool for reasoning about what each division does, which is what they are good for, and not as a complete taxonomy of what goes wrong in a human oocyte.

Check
id check-which-division
  1. In a first-division failure, how many of the four products have a normal chromosome count?
  2. A trisomic individual is homozygous at the centromere of the tripled chromosome for one of the mother's two versions. Which division failed?
  3. Why can a marker halfway along the chromosome arm not be used for that inference?
  4. Which of the two cases leaves two entirely normal gametes, and why does that follow from what the second division separates?

The single functional gamete of oogenesis comes from a 2019 review of sexually dimorphic meiotic prophase.

scenes.title: A well-documented effect with an unfinished explanation
scenes.contentHtml:
A well-documented effect with an unfinished explanation

Callout
id callout-boundary-age-scene

Teaching example, not medical advice. Every figure below is a population aggregate from a published study. None of them is anyone's personal risk, none is a threshold, and nothing here is a screening recommendation, a reproductive recommendation, or a statement about what any individual should do or expect. No individual is described. This scene is an exercise in reading evidence about a mechanism, and the mechanism is the subject rather than any decision.

Errors of the kind scene 5 modelled are not rare curiosities. Aneuploid embryos account for at least 10 per cent of human pregnancies. About 0.3 per cent of newborn infants are trisomic or monosomic, and about 35 per cent of spontaneous abortions are. For women nearing the end of their reproductive lifespan the incidence of aneuploidy may exceed 50 per cent.

Set beside the checkpoint stringency of spermatogenesis, where errors are described as extremely rare, those numbers make meiosis in the human female look like an unusually error-prone process. It is. The interesting question is why, and this scene is an audit of how well that question has been answered.

What is firmly established, and how firmly

One thing is established outright, and a second is established only in part. Separating those two is the work of this scene.

Established: aneuploidy rises with maternal age. This is about as well documented as anything in reproductive biology, from several independent kinds of study.

Established in direction, not in magnitude: the rise is not uniform across the two divisions. The 1996 study from scene 5 compared women aged 40 and over with women under 25, and reported the comparison as an odds ratio: a figure that sets the odds of the outcome in one group against the odds in the other, where 1 would mean no difference between them and a larger value means the outcome is concentrated in the older group.

For errors at the first maternal division the odds ratio was 5.2. For errors at the second maternal division it was 51.4.

That second pair of numbers is worth sitting with before drawing anything from it, because the size of the gap between 5.2 and 51.4 turns out to be much less secure than the fact that the two divisions behave differently.

What that study can and cannot establish

Investigation
id investigation-audit-the-age-evidence

Audit the design before you accept the inference.

That study assigned 170 trisomy 21 cases to a parental origin and a meiotic division using DNA sequence differences, then compared age bands. Ask three questions of it.

How many cases sit behind the striking number? Work it out. Of 170 cases, 86 per cent were maternal, which is about 146. Of those, 25 per cent were at the second division, which is about 37. That odds ratio of 51.4 rests on roughly 37 cases distributed across age bands. A large ratio computed from a small subgroup is a real finding and an imprecise one at the same time, and the size of the ratio is not evidence of the precision of the ratio.

Is it retrospective? Yes. It reads the DNA of children already born with trisomy 21 and infers backwards to a division that happened years earlier. It observes outcomes, not the meiosis itself.

What does the study's own conclusion claim? The authors state that the results support an association between advanced maternal age and errors at both divisions, that the association with the first division does not pinpoint when the error happened, and that the association with the second division implies at least one age-related mechanism acting around the time of conception.

Notice how carefully that is phrased. "Supports an association." "Does not pinpoint." "Implies at least one mechanism." The design can establish that age and stage travel together and can locate a mechanism in time. It cannot say what the mechanism is.

Three candidate mechanisms, and where each one stands

Cohesion weakening over the decades of arrest. This is the leading candidate and the one with the most direct evidence. The logic is attractive because scene 2 built it: cohesion is what holds sister chromatids together, and centromeric cohesion in particular has to survive from the first division to the second. In a female meiosis, scene 4 established, the cell has been holding that arrangement since before the woman was born. Protein glue asked to hold for four decades is a plausible thing to fail.

A 2019 study examined 218 oocytes from donors aged 9 to 43 and found that aneuploidy in eggs follows a U-shaped relation with age, high at both ends. Within that, it separated error patterns: precocious separation of sister chromatids increased linearly with age, while first-division non-disjunction actually decreased with age, and reverse segregation increased in the oldest group. The authors propose that cohesion weakening acts as a molecular clock limiting reproductive capacity, and they report a correlation between loss of centromeric cohesion and the pattern that rises with age.

Recombination failure. Studies in the 1990s identified failure to recombine, and crossovers in unhelpful positions, as prominent contributors to human trisomy. Scene 2 gives the mechanism directly: no crossover means no chiasma means nothing holding the pair. The scale is not trivial: over 10 per cent of all human oocytes contain at least one bivalent with no crossover.

Weak checkpoints. Scene 4's row about the poor checkpoint response in oogenesis belongs here too. A permissive checkpoint does not cause an error; it fails to catch one.

Where the explanation stops

Now the part that a textbook summary usually omits.

The 2012 review that collects this literature reaches a deliberately unfinished conclusion. It notes that the age curve for trisomy in natural conceptions is J-shaped, with a slight increase at the youngest maternal ages as well as an exponential increase in the decade before menopause, and that the shape of the curve differs between individual chromosomes. Its reading of that is that ageing affects chromosome segregation by multiple mechanisms rather than one. On the leading candidate specifically, it concludes that loss of cohesin seems unlikely to be the only force driving the steep rise before menopause. Its overall summary is that human aneuploidy arises through a multi-step process, with errors at several distinct stages of oogenesis, made worse by the absence of efficient checkpoints.

The 2019 study is equally explicit about its own limit. Having linked the age-rising pattern to cohesion, it says the mechanism causing the elevated first-division non-disjunction seen in young females is currently unclear. The U-shape has two arms and the study accounts for one of them.

Two studies that do not agree about the first division

There is a straight conflict between the two studies used in this scene, and it needs stating rather than stepping around.

The 1996 study reports first-division maternal errors becoming more common with age, at an odds ratio of 5.2. The 2019 study reports first-division non-disjunction decreasing with age. Both cannot be describing the same quantity.

They are not. Three differences are visible in what each one measured.

  • Different material. The 1996 study read trisomy 21 in infants who were born. The 2019 study examined oocytes directly. Anything that affects whether an affected conception survives to birth sits between those two.
  • Different chromosomes. The 1996 figures are for chromosome 21 alone. The 2019 figures are across all chromosomes, and scene 6's own review notes that age curves differ from chromosome to chromosome.
  • Different categories. The 2019 study splits first-division errors into three patterns and reports the trend for one of them, first-division non-disjunction, separately from the other two, both of which rise with age. The 1996 marker method does not use those categories at all, so "first-division error" does not name the same set of events in the two papers.

Any of those could account for the disagreement, and this lesson cannot say which does. What follows is that the direction of first-division errors with maternal age is not settled by putting these two studies side by side, and the earlier statement that the two divisions behave differently rests on the 1996 study alone.

So the honest state of the question:

Statement Status
Aneuploidy in human eggs and conceptions rises with maternal age Well documented, multiple independent designs
The two meiotic divisions behave differently with age Observed in the 1996 study; rests on that one design here
The second-division odds ratio is about 51 Direction supported, magnitude imprecise on roughly 37 cases
First-division errors become more common with age Unresolved: the two studies used here report opposite directions
Cohesion weakening during prolonged arrest contributes Leading candidate, with supporting correlation
Cohesion weakening is the sole or sufficient cause Explicitly doubted by the reviewing authors
Failure to recombine contributes Established as a contributor
One mechanism explains the whole age curve Contradicted by the shape of the curve itself
The elevated error rate at young maternal ages is explained Stated to be unclear

A learner who can reproduce that table has understood this material better than one who can recite "cohesion degrades with age." That recitation is defensible as far as it goes. What it gets wrong is the confidence: it presents as closed a question the literature leaves open.

A discrepancy this lesson could not resolve

One more piece of honesty, of the arithmetic kind.

Scene 3 reported that 2.60 per cent of bivalents in female material lacked a crossover marker. There are 23 bivalents per oocyte. If each were independent, the fraction of oocytes containing at least one such bivalent would be 1−(1−0.026)231 - (1 - 0.026)^{23}, which is about 45 per cent. The review quoted above puts the figure at over 10 per cent.

Those do not sit comfortably together, and this lesson does not know which is closer to the truth. Candidate explanations include the marker undercounting real crossovers, so that some bivalents scored as having none actually had one; the two figures coming from different populations, one of them fetal ovary material; and bivalents not being independent of one another. Both published figures are reported here as published, and the 45 per cent is what an independence assumption yields rather than a measured quantity.

Check

  1. Roughly how many maternal second-division cases sat behind the odds ratio of 51.4? What does that do to your confidence in the size of the ratio, and what does it leave untouched?
  2. The 2019 study found first-division non-disjunction decreasing with age. Why is that awkward for an explanation in which everything gets worse with time?
  3. The two studies report opposite directions for first-division errors with age. Give two differences in what they measured that could account for it.

scenes.title: Practice: trace it, count it, then say what failed
scenes.contentHtml:
Practice: trace it, count it, then say what failed

Five tasks, with the support falling away as you go. Task 1 tells you which method to use. By task 5 you are choosing the method yourself.

Task 1: trace one pair, with the steps named

A cell entering meiosis carries chromosome 15 from each parent. Replication has already happened.

Answer each part in one line, and the scene-2 headings tell you where to look for each.

  1. How many chromatids of chromosome 15 does the cell contain at this point?
  2. What is the paired structure of the two homologs called?
  3. At the first anaphase, which of the two connections is released, and what moves apart?
  4. Immediately after the first division, how many chromosome 15s does each product hold, and how many chromatids does each of those consist of?
  5. At the second anaphase, what is released and what moves apart?
  6. State which division was reductional and give the reason in terms of what it separated.

Task 2: the same counting, a different organism

A hypothetical animal has a diploid chromosome number of 16. A study counts crossover markers in its meiotic cells and reports a mean of 20 per cell.

  1. How many chromosome pairs does it have?
  2. How many combinations of whole chromosomes can independent assortment alone produce in one of its gametes?
  3. How many crossovers does that give per chromosome pair on average?
  4. Compare that per-pair figure with the human male figure from scene 3. Which of the two averages is lower?
  5. A colleague concludes from part 4 that the species with the lower average must therefore have more chromosome pairs that end up with no crossover at all. Scene 3 gives you a specific reason to refuse that inference, and a specific pair of human numbers that demonstrates it. State both, and say what you would need to measure instead.
  6. Quite apart from variation, why does it matter whether a pair receives a crossover?

Task 3: read a marker result

Three findings, each in a different individual with a trisomy. For each, name the division at which the error occurred, or say the result does not distinguish them. Use the two-case model from scene 5 and assume the marker sits at the centromere.

  1. At the centromere of the tripled chromosome, the individual carries two different maternal sequence variants and one paternal variant.
  2. At the centromere, the individual carries two identical copies of one maternal variant and one paternal variant.
  3. At a marker two-thirds of the way along the chromosome arm, the individual carries two different maternal variants.

Task 4: audit a sentence

Here is a sentence of the kind that appears in course notes:

"Cohesion between sister chromatids degrades over the decades an oocyte spends arrested, and this is why aneuploidy increases with maternal age."

Using scene 6 only, answer:

  1. Which part of that sentence is well supported?
  2. Which word in it goes beyond what the cited literature concludes?
  3. Name one published observation the sentence cannot accommodate.
  4. Rewrite the sentence so that it says only what the evidence supports.

Task 5: no method named

A colleague argues that because meiosis produces such large numbers of genetically distinct gametes, a tissue that divides as often as the colonic crypt must also be generating large genetic diversity among its cells over a lifetime.

Say whether the conclusion follows, and identify the specific step where the reasoning goes wrong. You are given no framework for this one; choose the parts of the lesson that apply.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every number and relationship in this lesson is available as prose, and no task requires seeing a picture.

The diagram in scene 2 has a long description carrying the same five stages, the same links and the same conclusion. The argument in that scene is complete without the picture: the section headed "Which separation happens first, and why the order is fixed" states the whole sequence in words, with all three counts at each step. If the diagram does not render or is not visible to you, read that section together with the long description.

Six tables appear in the lesson, in scenes 4, 5, 6 and 8, and each is restated in the sentences around it. The five rows of scene 4's comparison are discussed one group at a time in the paragraphs that follow it. The two product tables in scene 5 are derivable from the M and P notation described in prose immediately above them, and that notation uses subscripts which read aloud as "M one" and "M two". Scene 5's two-case summary, scene 6's status table and scene 8's meiosis-and-mitosis table all restate judgments that appear as full sentences nearby.

Every calculation is written out as an explicit arithmetic step with its result, including the powers of two, which are built up from 2 to the 10 instead of being assumed. A calculator is fine. Nothing is timed and no mental arithmetic is required. Nothing anywhere in the lesson depends on colour, motion or sound to carry its meaning.

Recovery route

If the two divisions keep collapsing into one another, stop trying to hold the sequence and hold one fact instead: there is only one glue, and the cell cuts it in two places at two times. Cohesion holds sister chromatids together along their arms and at their centromeres. Division one cuts the arm cohesion, and because the swapped arms beyond a crossover were being held by exactly that cohesion, cutting it also lets the chiasma go, so the homologs come apart. Division two cuts the centromeric cohesion, and only then do the sisters come apart. One glue, two locations, two times, in that order. Everything else in scene 2 hangs off it.

If you can say what each division separates but the arithmetic will not stay put, run one pass counting only DNA copies of a single chromosome. Start at four for the bivalent, go to two after the first division, and one after the second. Then check the chromosome count separately: 46 to 23 at the first division, and unchanged at the second. Two counts, falling at different steps, is the thing to hold.

If task 2 went wrong, the problem is probably that you used the diploid number where the number of pairs belongs. Independent assortment counts pairs, so the exponent is the count of pairs and never the count of chromosomes. Redo part 2 with 8 in the exponent and check it against the human case: 23 pairs gives 2 to the 23, and not 2 to the 46.

If the combinatorics in scene 3 did not land, the ratio work in PREM-QNT-005 on powers and orders of magnitude is the direct prerequisite, and lesson 01 of this block used the same arithmetic on cell sizes. Then re-run only step 1 of scene 3, which needs nothing but repeated doubling.

If task 4 felt like a trick, it was not. Separating a documented association from a proposed mechanism is a skill the earlier blocks teach directly: PREM-SCI-007 on correlation, causation and confounding, and PREM-SCI-011 on mechanistic and convergent evidence, both apply to it. Scene 6's status table is the worked version of that separation.

If task 5 went wrong, check whether you carried "variation" across from one setting to the other without noticing that it means two different things. Scene 8 is where that gets resolved, so reading it and returning to task 5 is a legitimate route rather than a shortcut.

If a whole scene refused to make sense on two passes, the likeliest reason is one of the two prerequisite gaps named at the end of scene 1. Neither is your fault and neither is recoverable by rereading this lesson. Ask your course text or instructor for the chromosome material rather than pressing on.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: in a crypt, a new combination is the other kind of problem
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: in a crypt, a new combination is the other kind of problem

Callout
id callout-boundary-wrap-up

Teaching example, not medical advice. The specimen described below is invented for this exercise. Nothing here is a diagnostic criterion, a threshold, a test performance, a screening or reproductive recommendation, a prognosis, or a statement of what any real finding would mean in any real person. No dose, no regimen and no management plan appears anywhere in this lesson. This is a reasoning exercise about which division produces which kind of chromosome error, worked with the tools the lesson has already built.

A laboratory receives a colonic biopsy. Among the epithelial cells it reports a population with an abnormal chromosome number: cells carrying three copies of one chromosome instead of two. The requesting note asks a reasonable-sounding question: could this be meiotic non-disjunction?

You can answer that with scene 1 alone, and the answer is no.

Working it

Step 1. Which division does this tissue perform? Meiosis is specialised for producing gametes. The crypt makes absorptive cells, goblet cells and their progenitors, and it makes them by somatic division. No cell in a colonic crypt is on its way to becoming a gamete, so no cell in a colonic crypt performs meiosis. Whatever produced those three copies, it was not a meiotic division of a crypt cell.

Step 2. So what are the possibilities? Two, and they are distinguished by when, not by where.

Either the error happened in a meiosis in a parent, or at fertilisation, in which case it is present in every cell of the body and the biopsy is showing you something constitutional that happens also to be in the colon. Or it happened in a mitotic division somewhere in that person's own lineage of crypt cells, in which case it is confined to the cells descended from the one that made the mistake.

Step 3. What would distinguish them? Whether the abnormal count is confined to a patch. A meiotic or fertilisation-stage error is in the whole person; a mitotic error in a crypt is in a clone. The reasoning is entirely from the lesson: meiosis happens once, before the individual exists, and everything after that is mitosis.

Step 4. Is the mitotic route actually real? It is, and scene 5 already showed the evidence in passing. In that population study of trisomy 21, 5 per cent of cases arose neither in maternal nor in paternal meiosis but by a mitotic error after fertilisation. Mitotic divisions do miscount chromosomes. The crypt performs an enormous number of them.

So the answer to the requesting note: the mechanism in scene 5 is the wrong mechanism for this tissue, and the question to ask instead is whether the finding is constitutional or clonal.

The reason this tissue must not do what meiosis does

Now the closing contrast, which is what this lesson has been building toward since its first paragraph.

Meiosis exists to produce new combinations. Scene 3 counted them: over eight million combinations of whole chromosomes from assortment alone, and many orders of magnitude more once crossing over is included. In the germ line, novelty is the product. The process is built to generate it, it breaks its own DNA on purpose to do so, and a meiosis that produced a gamete genetically identical to the parent cell would have failed at its job.

A crypt needs the opposite. A stem cell at the crypt base has to make daughters that carry what it carried. The tissue works because the cells are the same. Genetic novelty in a crypt is not a product; it is damage.

And the crypt's exposure to that damage scales with exactly the thing lesson 01 opened with: how much dividing it does. Across tissues, cancer risk is correlated with the number of stem-cell divisions a tissue requires to maintain itself, because more divisions carry more opportunity for random mutations to accumulate. The colon renews every three to five days for a lifetime. The bill for that comes due in lesson 10.

The two divisions side by side

Everything needed for the comparison is now in place, so here it is in one piece. Read the last row first: it is the row the whole lesson has been about.

Mitosis Meiosis
Do homologs pair? No. They behave independently and are never matched up. Yes. Each pairs with its partner into a bivalent of four chromatids, tied by a chiasma.
What separates? Sister chromatids, in one division. Homologs at division I, then sister chromatids at division II.
Chromosome number Unchanged: 46 in, 46 in each product. Halved, and only at division I: 46 to 23.
DNA copies per chromosome Two before, one in each product. Two after division I, one after division II.
Product Two cells matching the parent, still diploid. Four haploid products in spermatogenesis; one egg plus polar bodies in oogenesis.

The two middle rows are the whole difference. Mitosis has one separation to make and meiosis has two, and it is the extra one, the separating of partners, that halves the chromosome number and reassorts the parents' contributions on the way.

So the same word, variation, names an achievement in one lineage and a hazard in the other, and the difference is not in the chromosomes. It is in what the tissue is for.

What this lesson did and did not settle

Three things it established. Meiosis halves the chromosome number by separating homologs at its first division and sister chromatids at its second, in that order, because two different connections have to be undone. The variation it produces is countable, and assortment alone gives 2 to the 23. A failure at each division leaves a different signature, and that signature can be read backwards from a centromere marker.

Three things it did not. It did not establish the mechanism of the maternal-age effect, because the literature has not; scene 6 records what is documented and what remains open. It did not resolve the discrepancy between two published figures for how many oocytes carry a crossover-less bivalent. And it did not teach mitosis or the cell cycle, which belong to PREM-05.08, or chromosome structure and genome organisation, which belong to PREM-06.02.

Lesson 10 of this block takes up cell death, senescence and cancer, and returns to the crypt when the climb stops ending.

Check
id check-wrap-up
  1. A trisomy is found in a patch of colonic epithelium and nowhere else in the body. Which kind of division produced it, and how do you know it was not meiotic?
  2. Give the one-sentence reason a colonic crypt could not use meiosis even if it had the machinery.
  3. "Meiosis generates variation and that is good; mitosis copies faithfully and that is also good." Explain why both halves are true, in terms of what each tissue is for.
