assessment.title: Meiosis, countable variation, and which division failed

items.prompt: A human diploid cell holds 23 homologous pairs. Counting only which member of each pair a gamete receives, and ignoring crossing over entirely, how many distinct combinations can independent assortment alone produce among one person's gametes? Give the exact whole number.

answer.reasoning:
Each pair contributes one of its two members, and the choice is independent for every pair, so the count is 2 multiplied by itself once per pair: 2 to the 23. Building it up, 2 to the 10 is 1024, so 2 to the 20 is 1024 squared, or 1,048,576, and multiplying by 2 to the 3 gives 8,388,608.

The exponent is the number of pairs, which is 23, and not the number of chromosomes, which is 46. Both numbers appear in the stem and only one of them belongs in the exponent.

Markers should note what this number is and is not. It is an exact count of the patterns of parental origin across the 23 centromeres, because a reciprocal exchange swaps material beyond the point of exchange and leaves each chromatid's own centromere in place. It is not an estimate of total gamete diversity, since it ignores crossing over. Do not withhold credit from a learner who adds that caveat, and do not require it: the item asks for a number.
commonErrors: Answering 2 to the 46, about 7.0 x 10^13, by using the diploid chromosome number as the exponent instead of the number of pairs. That figure is the count for a couple's zygotes, not for one person's gametes.
Answering 46 or 23 by multiplying instead of exponentiating.
Adding crossovers into this count. The stem excludes them explicitly.

items.prompt: A cytological study measured a mean of 49.09 crossover foci per cell in human male meiosis. A human cell has 23 chromosome pairs. Compute the mean number of crossovers per chromosome pair, to two decimal places.

answer.summary: 2.13. The genome-wide mean divided by the number of pairs: 49.09 divided by 23.
answer.reasoning:
The 49.09 is a whole-genome count per cell, and the 23 pairs share it, so the per-pair mean is 49.09 divided by 23, which is 2.134 and rounds to 2.13. Both numbers are supplied in the stem and the division is the whole of the required work.

What the number is good for is worth stating for the marker. An average above 1 per pair is consistent with almost every pair receiving at least one crossover, which matters because a pair with no crossover has no chiasma holding it together. What the average does not do is tell you the failure rate: the measured frequency of bivalents with no crossover marker is 0.38 per cent in males and 2.60 per cent in females, and the female has both the higher average and the higher failure rate. Do not award or withhold credit for any claim about that; the item asks for a division.
commonErrors: Dividing by 46 instead of 23 and answering about 1.07. That would be crossovers per chromosome rather than per pair, and the foci are counted per bivalent.
Inverting the division and answering about 0.47.
Treating 2.13 as a guarantee that every pair receives a crossover. It is a mean, and the measured proportion of bivalents with none is small but not zero.

items.prompt: Put these five stages of one meiosis into the order in which they occur, beginning with the earliest.

options.text: Centromeric cohesion is released, and the sister chromatids of each chromosome move apart.
Each replicated chromosome pairs with its replicated homolog, forming a bivalent of four chromatids.
Four products exist, each holding 23 chromosomes of one chromatid each.
The DNA is replicated, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
Cohesion along the chromatid arms is released, and the two homologs move to opposite poles.

answer.summary: Replication, then pairing into a bivalent, then arm cohesion released with homologs separating, then centromeric cohesion released with sister chromatids separating, then four haploid products.
answer.reasoning:
Replication comes first, because a bivalent is defined as two *replicated* homologs paired and so cannot form before the copying has happened. Pairing follows.

The two cohesion steps are in a fixed order and that order is the substance of the lesson. Arm cohesion is degraded at the start of the first anaphase, which lets the homologs move to opposite poles; centromeric cohesion is held by cohesins specific to meiosis and is degraded only at the second division, which is when sister chromatids finally come apart. Reversing those two would separate copies before partners had been sorted, and would sort nothing.

The four products come last. Note that four products is the count of what the two divisions yield; in oogenesis only one of them becomes the functional gamete and the others are polar bodies, which does not change the order of the stages.

The options are deliberately presented out of order in the option list, so a learner cannot recover the answer from the order they are displayed in.
acceptableResponses: replication; bivalent; arm cohesion and homologs separate; centromeric cohesion and sisters separate; four products
commonErrors: Swapping the two cohesion steps, so that sister chromatids separate at the first division. That is the single most common error in this material and it makes the first division equational, which would leave the chromosome number unhalved.
Placing pairing before replication. A bivalent contains four chromatids, so replication has already happened by the time it forms.
Placing the four products immediately after the first division. The first division yields two products, each still holding two chromatids per chromosome.

items.prompt: Reason inside the two-case model this lesson built, in which exactly one chromosome pair fails to separate at exactly one of the two meiotic divisions, no other error occurs, and the sequence marker examined lies at the centromere. A trisomic individual carries, at the centromere of the tripled chromosome, two different sequence variants inherited from the mother together with one from the father. Within that model, which division failed?

options.text: The result cannot distinguish between the two maternal divisions

answer.summary: Maternal meiosis I. Two different maternal centromere variants mean the extra chromosome came from two different maternal homologs, and only a first-division failure sends both homologs into one product.
answer.reasoning:
The mother's two homologs differ in sequence, because they came from her two parents. Her two sister chromatids of either homolog are identical to each other, because one was copied from the other.

So: a first-division failure sends both maternal homologs into the same product, and that product carries two chromosomes with different centromere sequence. A second-division failure sends two sister copies of a single homolog into one product, and that product carries two chromosomes with identical centromere sequence. The individual described has two different maternal variants, which matches the first case.

The extra chromosome is maternal, since it is the mother's contribution that is doubled and only one paternal variant is present, so the paternal option is excluded. The indeterminate option is wrong within the stated model, because within that model the two cases give different marker results, and this is the method published studies use: origin is assigned by centromeric heterozygosity or homozygosity.

Three limits the marker should hold in mind, none of which changes the key. The marker has to be centromeric: crossing over exchanges material along the arms, so a marker further out may have moved between homologs and would no longer report where the centromere came from. The stem stipulates a centromeric marker for that reason. Second, the model is a simplification of human oogenesis, where patterns exist in which sister chromatids separate at the first division; the stem confines the question to the model. Third, a trisomy can also arise from a mitotic error after fertilisation, which the stem excludes by stipulating a meiotic failure. Award full credit for the keyed option; treat a learner who names any of these three limits as showing additional understanding rather than as hedging.
acceptableResponses: the first meiotic division, in the mother
commonErrors: Choosing maternal meiosis II by associating 'two copies' with sister chromatids without checking whether the two centromere variants are the same or different. Two copies of one homolog would be identical at the centromere.

Choosing the indeterminate option on the grounds that human oocytes show more than two error patterns. That is true of real oocytes and is discussed in the lesson, but the stem restricts the question to the two-case model.
Choosing a paternal origin. Only one paternal variant is present, so the paternal contribution is not the doubled one.

items.prompt: In a spermatogenesis, one chromosome pair fails to separate at the first meiotic division, so both of its homologs pass into the same daughter cell. The second division then proceeds normally in both daughter cells, and no other chromosome pair is affected. Of the four products, how many carry an abnormal number of that chromosome?

answer.summary: All four. Two products carry two copies of that chromosome and two carry none.
answer.reasoning:
Label the maternal homolog's sister chromatids M1 and M2 and the paternal homolog's P1 and P2.

The first division sends both homologs one way, so one daughter cell holds M1, M2, P1 and P2, and the other holds no copy of that chromosome. The second division then separates sister chromatids normally in both. In the first daughter cell that gives one product with M1 and P1 and another with M2 and P2, each carrying two copies. In the second daughter cell there is nothing of that chromosome to separate, so both of its products carry none.

Two products with two copies and two with none is four abnormal products out of four. The contrast with a second-division failure, which leaves two entirely normal products, is the point of the pair of items.

The stem specifies spermatogenesis so that all four products are countable gametes. In oogenesis the same divisions occur but only one product becomes the egg and the rest are polar bodies, so the number of abnormal *products* would be unchanged while the number of abnormal gametes would depend on which product was retained. Accept 4 on the stated stem; a learner who notes that distinction has understood more, not less.
commonErrors: Answering 2 by counting only the products that gained a chromosome and forgetting that the products which received none are also abnormal.
Answering 2 by importing the result for a second-division failure, where two products are normal.
Answering 1, which would require the failure to affect only one of the two daughter cells; a first-division failure affects both, because whatever one cell gains the other lacks.

items.prompt: In a spermatogenesis, the first meiotic division separates one chromosome pair correctly, but in one of the two daughter cells the sister chromatids of that chromosome fail to separate at the second division. The other daughter cell divides normally, and no other chromosome pair is affected. Of the four products, how many carry an abnormal number of that chromosome?

answer.summary: Two. One product carries two copies of the same homolog and one carries none; the other two products are normal.
answer.reasoning:
Using the same labels, the first division works, so one daughter cell holds M1 and M2 and the other holds P1 and P2.

In the cell where the second division fails, both M1 and M2 pass into one product and the other product receives none. That is one product with two copies and one with none. The cell holding P1 and P2 divides normally and yields two products with one copy each.

So two of the four products are abnormal and two are entirely normal. This is the structural difference from a first-division failure, where all four products are affected, and it follows from what each division separates: a second-division failure can only spoil the output of the one daughter cell in which it happens.

The two copies in the abnormal product are M1 and M2, which are identical to each other, and that is why a second-division failure leaves a homozygous signature at the centromere while a first-division failure leaves a heterozygous one.
commonErrors: Answering 4 by importing the result for a first-division failure. A second-division failure is confined to one of the two daughter cells.
Answering 1 by counting only the product that gained a chromosome and not the one that received none.
Answering 2 but describing the extra copies as two different homologs. They are sister chromatids of one homolog, and that difference is what a centromere marker reads.

items.prompt: Select every statement that the evidence cited in this lesson supports as written. Do not select a statement that claims more than the cited sources do.

options.text: Aneuploidy in human eggs and in human conceptions rises with maternal age.

Weakening of sister-chromatid cohesion during the long prophase arrest has been proposed as a contributor, and one study reports a correlation between loss of centromeric cohesion and an error pattern that rises with age.
Cohesion weakening is now established as the cause of the maternal age effect.
Failure to recombine has been identified as a contributor to human trisomy.
The raised rate of first-division non-disjunction seen in young women is explained by cohesion weakening.
A single mechanism accounts for the whole shape of the maternal age curve.

answer.summary: The association with age, the cohesion account stated as a proposal with a supporting correlation, and recombination failure as a contributor. The other three claim more than the cited sources do.
answer.reasoning:
Taking the three keyed options first. The rise with maternal age is documented by several independent designs cited in the lesson, including a retrospective population study and a study of 218 oocytes that found a U-shaped relation with age. The cohesion option is worded as a proposal with a reported correlation, which is exactly what the 2019 study offers: it proposes cohesion weakening as a molecular clock and reports a correlation with the error pattern that rises with age. Recombination failure is identified as a prominent contributor to human trisomy by the 2012 review, which also gives the figure of over 10 per cent of oocytes carrying at least one crossover-less bivalent.

Now the three that must not be selected. That cohesion weakening is the established cause is contradicted by the reviewing authors of the 2012 paper, who conclude that loss of cohesin seems unlikely to be the only force driving the rise before menopause; a proposal with a supporting correlation is not an established cause. That the young-age pattern is explained by cohesion weakening is contradicted directly by the 2019 authors, who state that a separate and currently unclear mechanism causes the elevated first-division non-disjunction in young females. That a single mechanism accounts for the whole curve is contradicted by the J-shaped curve having effects at both extremes and by the age curves differing between individual chromosomes, which the review reads as pointing to multiple mechanisms.

The discrimination this item tests is between a proposal and a finding. The two wordings differ only in their epistemic verb, and a learner who selects the strong version has read the mechanism as settled when the literature does not.
commonErrors: Selecting the statement that cohesion weakening is the established cause. It is the leading candidate and it is not established; one cited review explicitly doubts that it is sufficient on its own.
Selecting the statement about young women. The study that reports that pattern says the mechanism behind it is currently unclear.

Selecting the single-mechanism statement. The curve rises at both extremes of reproductive life and differs between chromosomes, which is the reviewing authors' reason for inferring more than one mechanism.
Declining to select the cohesion proposal because it is not settled. It is worded as a proposal with a reported correlation, and that is supported as written.

items.prompt: A revision card reads: "One meiosis produces four gametes." Name the process for which that is accurate, say what happens instead in the other, and give the number of functional gametes one meiosis yields there.

answer.correct: Accurate for spermatogenesis, where both divisions are symmetrical and one meiosis yields four functional gametes. In oogenesis both divisions are asymmetric: half the genome is segregated into polar bodies, so one meiosis yields one functional gamete.
answer.summary: True of spermatogenesis, which gives four. Oogenesis divides asymmetrically into polar bodies and gives one.
answer.reasoning:
Full credit requires three things: naming spermatogenesis as the accurate case, identifying the asymmetric division into polar bodies as what happens in oogenesis, and giving one as the number of functional gametes from a female meiosis.

The number of functional gametes is the load-bearing part. Award the mark for one. Do not require a specific number of polar bodies: the source this lesson follows describes two, one per division, while other accounts give three, and the lesson records that disagreement rather than settling it. A learner who says two, three, or simply 'the rest are polar bodies' should not lose credit on that point.

Accept 'sperm production' or 'the male' for spermatogenesis and 'egg production' or 'the female' for oogenesis. Do not accept an answer that says four in both cases, and do not accept one that says the female produces four gametes of which some die: the polar bodies are products of the divisions and are not functional gametes.
acceptableResponses: Accurate for spermatogenesis, which gives four functional gametes. Oogenesis divides asymmetrically, discarding half the genome into polar bodies, and yields one functional gamete.
True in the male: four sperm. In the female, the divisions are lopsided and produce polar bodies, so only one egg results from each meiosis.
Spermatogenesis, four. Oogenesis produces one egg plus polar bodies.
commonErrors: Saying four in both cases, which is the error the card contains.
Saying the female also makes four gametes but three of them die. The polar bodies are not gametes that then die; the divisions are asymmetric and only one product is a functional gamete.
Naming the right numbers without naming which process each belongs to, which leaves the card uncorrected.

items.prompt: A colleague argues that because meiosis produces such large numbers of genetically distinct gametes, a tissue that divides as often as the colonic crypt must be generating comparable genetic diversity among its own cells over a lifetime. In four or five sentences, say whether the conclusion follows, identify the step at which the reasoning fails, and contrast what new genetic combinations mean in the germ line with what new genetic differences mean in a crypt.

answer.correct: The conclusion does not follow. It assumes that any frequently dividing tissue runs the process that generates the diversity, but a crypt divides mitotically and mitosis neither pairs homologs nor recombines them: it separates sister chromatids and produces daughters carrying what the parent carried. Meiosis, which does pair and recombine, happens only in the germ line, and no crypt cell is on the path to becoming a gamete. So in the germ line new combinations are the product, generated deliberately, while in a crypt a new genetic difference can only be an error in copying, and the tissue works because its cells are the same. That is why division load in a somatic tissue is discussed as a route to accumulating random mutations rather than as a source of useful variety.
answer.summary: It does not follow. Frequent division is mitotic, and mitosis copies rather than recombining; meiosis is confined to the germ line. Variation is the germ line's product and a crypt's defect.
answer.reasoning:
The reasoning fails at a specific step, and credit should turn on whether the learner locates it: the argument treats 'divides a lot' as though it implied 'runs meiosis'. Frequency of division says nothing about which kind of division.

A full answer names what mitosis does and does not do. It separates sister chromatids, which are identical copies, so its output is two cells carrying what the parent carried; it does not bring homologs together, so it cannot assort them independently and it does not recombine them. Both mechanisms this lesson counted, independent assortment and crossing over, act on paired homologs at the first meiotic division and have no counterpart in a mitotic division.

A full answer also names the germ-line restriction: meiosis is specialised for producing gametes and occurs only in the lineage that makes them, and crypt cells are somatic.

The contrast should come out as an asymmetry of purpose rather than of chromosomes. In the germ line, novelty is the product; a meiosis producing a gamete identical to the parent cell would have failed. In a crypt, the cells work because they are alike, so a new genetic difference is damage. Accept an answer that connects the crypt's division load to accumulating random mutation, which is how the cited review frames the correlation with cancer risk across tissues, provided the learner keeps it as a correlation across tissues and does not turn it into a risk claim about a person.

Do not require the learner to discuss cancer at all; the outcome being assessed is the somatic-versus-germ-line contrast. Do not credit an answer that agrees with the colleague, and do not credit one that rejects the conclusion only by asserting that crypt cells 'do not do meiosis' without saying what mitosis does instead.
acceptableResponses: No. The crypt divides mitotically, and mitosis separates sister chromatids rather than pairing and recombining homologs, so it copies instead of reassorting. Meiosis is confined to the germ line and no crypt cell becomes a gamete. New combinations are the germ line's whole product; in a crypt a new genetic difference is a copying error, and the tissue depends on its cells being alike.

The conclusion fails because it confuses how often a tissue divides with which division it performs. Independent assortment and crossing over both act on paired homologs at meiosis I, and mitosis never pairs homologs. So the crypt's many divisions generate no reassortment by design; any genetic difference there is damage rather than variety.
commonErrors: Agreeing that many divisions must yield much diversity. Division count is unrelated to whether homologs are paired and recombined.
Rejecting the conclusion by asserting that somatic cells do not undergo meiosis, without saying what mitosis separates and therefore why no reassortment occurs.
Claiming a crypt generates no genetic differences at all. Mitotic errors and random mutations do occur; the point is that they are errors rather than a designed product.
Turning the tissue-level correlation between stem-cell division load and cancer risk into a statement about an individual's risk. It is a correlation across tissue types.

claims.uncertainty: The renewal figure is a bulk population interval and not a claim that every cell is replaced together; cell-type lifetimes vary and self-renewing lineages persist, and the same source notes that some enteroendocrine cells can persist for up to 28 days. The stem-cell count and the division interval come from reviews of the intestinal niche and are approximate.

claims.statement: Mitosis is a type of cell division for somatic cells, whereas meiosis is a specialised style of cell division conserved in eukaryotes and particularly designed for the production of gametes; in mitosis the maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes behave independently upon segregation, while in meiosis homologous chromosomes are paired and some of them are physically connected by chiasmata.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic cell division in general. This is the minimum account of mitosis the meiosis comparison needs, sourced independently by this lesson; PREM-05.08 owns the account of mitosis, the cell cycle and their machinery, and this lesson neither extends nor anticipates it.
claims.uncertainty: The statement is a general framing from a review rather than a measurement. That meiosis is restricted to the germ line follows from its role in gamete production as stated here and is not separately measured by this source.

claims.statement: An ordinary mitotic division separates sister chromatids, the two identical copies produced when a chromosome was replicated, sending one to each daughter cell, so that each daughter receives the same chromosome number the parent cell held.
claims.scope: Mitotic division in eukaryotic somatic cells, stated only to the depth the comparison with meiosis requires. PREM-05.08 owns mitosis.
claims.uncertainty: The sources establish that mitosis separates sister chromatids and that sister kinetochores are bi-oriented; the consequence that the chromosome number is preserved is the arithmetic of that separation rather than a separately measured claim.

claims.statement: The human euploid genome contains 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs, and a balanced chromosome number of this kind is called euploid.
claims.scope: The standard human karyotype. This is a diploid count of a somatic cell and is compatible with PREM-BIO-002's statement that the reference human genome assembly spans 22 autosomes and chromosome X, which describes one haploid assembled sequence rather than a diploid chromosome count.
claims.uncertainty: None material for the teaching use here. Individuals with variant karyotypes exist, which is the subject of the aneuploidy claims in this same lesson.

claims.statement: Meiosis consists of a single phase of DNA replication followed by two cell divisions, with no further round of replication between the two divisions.
claims.scope: Meiosis in eukaryotes generally, as presented in a cell-biology textbook chapter.
claims.uncertainty: None material. The lesson is explicit that this replication is an observed feature taken as given, and that the requirement for two divisions follows from it by counting rather than standing as an independent necessity; why meiosis replicates first is not addressed by this source or by the lesson.

claims.statement: During meiosis each duplicated chromosome pairs with its duplicated homolog to form a structure called a bivalent, which contains four chromatids; the two homologs are similar but not identical in DNA sequence, whereas the two sister chromatids of one homolog are identical copies.
claims.scope: Meiotic prophase in eukaryotes.
claims.uncertainty: How the two homologs locate each other in the nucleus is not established by this source and is explicitly left unexplained by the lesson rather than glossed over.

claims.statement: At anaphase of the first meiotic division the two duplicated homologs, each still consisting of two sister chromatids, separate from each other and move to opposite spindle poles; at anaphase of the second meiotic division the sister chromatids separate, producing cells with a haploid DNA content.
claims.scope: The two meiotic divisions in eukaryotes. This is the central factual claim of the lesson and the basis of the reductional and equational labels, which the lesson attaches to the arithmetic rather than taking as vocabulary from this source; the source does not use those two words.
claims.uncertainty: None material for the normal case. The lesson separately records, from a different source, that human oocytes show patterns in which sister chromatids separate at the first division, so this description is the normal course of events rather than an exhaustive account of what can happen.

claims.statement: Cohesion between sister chromatids is released in two stages: the arms of sister chromatids become unglued at the start of anaphase I when the cohesins holding the arms together are degraded, while the sister chromatids of each duplicated homolog remain attached at the centromere by meiosis-specific cohesins that are degraded only at anaphase of meiotic division II.
claims.scope: Meiotic sister-chromatid cohesion in eukaryotes. The lesson presents cohesion as one substance released in two stages at two locations, which is what this source describes, rather than as two different kinds of connection.
claims.uncertainty: The source names arm and centromeric cohesins without giving the full protein inventory or the protection mechanism, and the lesson does not assert one.

claims.statement: The chiasmata created by crossover events hold the maternal and paternal homologs together until the spindle separates them at anaphase I; in organisms with a reduced frequency of meiotic crossing over some chromosome pairs lack chiasmata, those pairs fail to segregate normally, and many of the resulting gametes contain too many or too few chromosomes.
claims.scope: Meiotic segregation in eukaryotes. The second half of the statement is framed by the source around mutant organisms with reduced crossing-over frequency, and the lesson keeps that framing rather than converting it into a general human claim; the corresponding human figures are carried by separate claims from cytological and review sources.
claims.uncertainty: The consequence for gametes is stated qualitatively by the source as many resulting gametes being affected, without a quantitative rate.

claims.statement: Releasing cohesion along the chromatid arms is what allows a chiasma to stop holding a pair of homologs together, because beyond the point of exchange the swapped arms are held to their neighbours by that arm cohesion.
claims.scope: Offered as this lesson's reading of two statements that sit adjacent in one textbook chapter: that chiasmata hold homologs together until anaphase I, and that arm cohesins are degraded at the start of anaphase I. The causal link between the two is the lesson's inference.
claims.uncertainty: No source consulted by this run states the causal link in these terms. It is a mechanistically standard reading, and the lesson marks it in prose as a reading rather than a quotation, but a reviewer should treat it as unsourced and may require it to be narrowed or removed.

claims.statement: During meiotic pairing the homologs exchange segments of DNA with each other, and where the exchange is reciprocal the two homologs end up physically connected at that point; genetic reassortment is enhanced by this crossing over beyond what the assortment of whole homologs alone provides.
claims.scope: Meiotic recombination in eukaryotes.
claims.uncertainty: The further step the lesson takes from this claim, that a reciprocal exchange leaves each chromatid's own centromere in place so that 2 to the 23 counts patterns of centromere parental origin exactly, is the lesson's reasoning from the reciprocal nature of the exchange and is identified as such in the scene 3 source note. No source states it.

claims.statement: In mitosis the sister kinetochores built on the core centromeres of sister chromatids are oppositely oriented in a back-to-back manner and bi-oriented, whereas in meiosis the orientation is converted to mono-orientation with the sister kinetochores united side by side, and this mono-orientation is essential for establishing the reductional division of meiosis I.
claims.scope: The geometric contrast between mitotic bi-orientation and meiosis I mono-orientation, stated generally in a review comparing the two divisions.
claims.uncertainty: The molecular components the review names as imposing mono-orientation, including Rec8, Moa1 and Meikin with shugoshin recruitment, are established largely in fission yeast. The lesson uses only the geometric contrast and bounds the molecular account in a learner-visible callout; it does not assert that the same protein mechanism operates in human meiosis.

claims.statement: The random distribution of maternal and paternal homologs between the daughter cells at meiotic division I means that from this process alone one individual could in principle produce 2 to the power n genetically different gametes, where n is the haploid number of chromosomes, and in humans that is at least 2 to the 23, about 8.4 million.
claims.scope: Independent assortment of whole homologs in human meiosis. The source's own phrase is at least 2 to the 23, because assortment is one of two mechanisms and crossing over adds further variation.
claims.uncertainty: The figure counts combinations of parental origin and does not account for crossing over. The lesson's further figures derived from it, namely 2 to the 46 for a couple, about 24 switch points per gamete and a 2-to-the-47 upper bound, are the lesson's own arithmetic under stated assumptions and are not supported by this or any other source.

claims.statement: In human meiosis the mean number of MLH1 crossover foci per cell was 49.09 with a standard error of 0.07 in males, across 4660 spermatocytes from 56 testicular biopsies, and 69.25 with a standard error of 0.29 in females, across 2038 oocytes from 63 fetal ovaries; the same study calculated genome-wide genetic lengths of 2455 cM in males and 3463 cM in females from those counts.
claims.scope: Human male and female meiotic cells in one cytological study. The female material is fetal ovarian tissue, so the female counts describe oocytes at a fetal stage rather than oocytes at ovulation.
claims.uncertainty: MLH1 foci are a marker for crossover sites and a focus count can undercount crossovers the marker does not label. The two map lengths are not independent measurements: the study calculated them from the focus counts using a 50 cM per crossover conversion, and its own authors note that linkage studies, which measure map length differently, report longer maps. A second study reports crossover numbers of about 50 and about 70 per nucleus in the two sexes, consistent with these.

claims.statement: The frequency of bivalents lacking an MLH1 crossover focus in human meiotic cells differed significantly between the sexes, at 0.38 per cent in males against 2.60 per cent in females.
claims.scope: Per-bivalent frequencies in the same cytological study, from male testicular biopsies and female fetal ovarian tissue.
claims.uncertainty: These are marker-based frequencies, so a bivalent scored as lacking a focus may have had a crossover the marker missed. The lesson notes explicitly that compounding this per-bivalent figure across 23 bivalents under an independence assumption yields about 45 per cent of oocytes carrying at least one such bivalent, which does not sit comfortably with a review's figure of over 10 per cent; the lesson reports both published figures and declines to resolve the discrepancy or to use its own 45 per cent for anything further.

claims.statement: In the same cytological study the mean number of RAD51 foci per cell, marking early recombination intermediates, was 134.07 with a standard error of 5.47 in males from 44 spermatocytes, and 250.28 with a standard error of 10.21 in females from 39 oocytes.
claims.scope: Early recombination-intermediate marker counts in one study, on small numbers of cells: 44 spermatocytes and 39 oocytes, far fewer than the thousands of cells behind that study's crossover counts.
claims.uncertainty: A second study reports higher figures of about 200 per nucleus in males and about 400 in females, roughly half again as many in each sex. The lesson reports both as a disagreement rather than averaging them, and uses only the direction both agree on, namely a large excess of breaks over crossovers and more of both in the female.

claims.statement: In human female meiosis about 25 per cent of the recombinational interactions designated to become crossovers never become crossovers, giving a crossover maturation efficiency of about 0.75 against about 1.0 in the male; double-strand breaks average about 200 per nucleus in males and about 400 in females; and the coefficient of variation for crossover number per nucleus is 18 per cent in females, 1.8-fold that in males at 10 per cent.
claims.scope: Human male and female meiosis as analysed in one 2017 study combining cytological and genetic data.
claims.uncertainty: Maturation efficiency is inferred from the relationship between designated precursor sites and final crossovers rather than observed directly for individual sites. The break counts disagree with an earlier study's lower figures. The lesson uses the variability and inefficiency findings to account for a pattern that a mean alone cannot explain; that use is the lesson's own argument and is not presented in the source.

claims.statement: During oogenesis the chromosomes undergo an asymmetrical division with half the genome segregated into polar bodies, producing only a single viable gamete, whereas spermatogenesis undergoes symmetrical divisions and produces four viable gametes.
claims.scope: Mammalian oogenesis and spermatogenesis, as contrasted in a review of sexually dimorphic meiotic prophase.
claims.uncertainty: The number of polar bodies is not settled by this claim. A separate source describes two, one from each division, and the lesson reports two on that basis while explicitly recording that other accounts give three; whether the first polar body divides again was not established by this run.

claims.statement: Oocytes are formed from primordial germ cells in the fetal ovary and commit in a one-way journey into meiosis, then arrest at the germinal-vesicle stage and spend the majority of their life having entered meiosis without completing it; the first meiotic division is very asymmetric and produces a mature egg together with a much smaller first polar body that later degenerates, after which the egg re-arrests at metaphase of meiosis II, and fertilisation is the event that triggers completion of meiosis II with the production of a second polar body.
claims.scope: Mammalian oocytes and eggs.
claims.uncertainty: The source does not state a maximum duration for the human prophase arrest; the decades figure used in the lesson comes from the separate review cited for the timing dimorphism. Only two polar bodies are described.

claims.statement: In mammals oogenesis occurs during fetal development in utero, with oocytes eventually arresting and being maintained in late prophase I for decades, whereas spermatogenesis occurs throughout the lifespan of the organism.
claims.scope: Mammalian meiosis, in a review of sexually dimorphic features of meiotic prophase.
claims.uncertainty: Decades is the source's own qualitative term rather than a measured interval for any individual.

claims.statement: During meiosis I in oocytes the spindle assembly checkpoint appears weak and ineffectual at detecting chromosomal alignment abnormalities compared with its activity during mitosis, and across the sexes the checkpoints during spermatogenesis are stringent enough that errors are extremely rare while during oogenesis the response of checkpoints to errors is very poor.
claims.scope: Mammalian oocyte and spermatocyte meiosis, drawn from two reviews.
claims.uncertainty: Both statements are qualitative comparisons offered in review prose rather than quantified detection rates. A permissive checkpoint permits an error rather than causing one, and the lesson states that distinction explicitly instead of treating weak checkpoints as a cause of aneuploidy.

claims.statement: Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate normally into the four haploid cells during meiosis, so that some of the resulting haploid cells lack a chromosome while others have more than one copy; Down syndrome in humans is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 resulting from non-disjunction during meiotic division I or II.
claims.scope: Definition and one named human example, from a cell-biology textbook chapter. Named here only to define a mechanism and its best-known consequence.
claims.uncertainty: The source attributes the extra chromosome 21 to non-disjunction at division I or II without apportioning between them; the apportionment used by the lesson comes from a separate population study, which also records a post-fertilisation mitotic category that this definitional claim does not cover.

claims.statement: Aneuploidy is an unbalanced change in chromosome number at the cellular or organismal level, in which certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs; trisomy means a diploid genome gained an additional chromosome, written 2N+1, and monosomy means a diploid genome lost one, written 2N-1; whole-chromosome aneuploidy involves entire chromosomes being gained or lost, as distinct from segmental aneuploidy in which pieces of chromosomes are amplified or deleted.
claims.scope: Definitions of chromosome-number terminology, taken from the terminology section of a review.
claims.uncertainty: None material. The lesson uses only the definitions and the chromosome count from this source and none of its claims about tumour biology.

claims.statement: Studies of the origin of trisomies in naturally occurring pregnancies use centromeric heterozygosity or homozygosity in the trisomic individual to infer the meiotic stage at which the error occurred.
claims.scope: The retrospective method used to assign a meiotic stage to a naturally occurring trisomy, as described in a review of human aneuploidy. The markers are centromeric.
claims.uncertainty: The review states the method without listing its failure modes. The lesson explains in prose why a marker distant from the centromere cannot serve, which is the lesson's own derivation from the exchange of segments during crossing over. The lesson also records, from a separate study, that human oocytes show error patterns in which sister chromatids separate at meiosis I; that study does not state whether such patterns are misclassified by this method, and the lesson makes no claim that they are.

claims.statement: Among 170 infants with trisomy 21 ascertained in a population-based study in metropolitan Atlanta between 1989 and 1993, with origin assigned using DNA polymorphisms, the distribution by origin was 86 per cent maternal, of which 75 per cent arose at meiosis I and 25 per cent at meiosis II, 9 per cent paternal split evenly between the two divisions, and 5 per cent mitotic.
claims.scope: One geographically defined cohort of 170 cases ascertained in the early 1990s. These are proportions within that cohort and are not universal constants; a different population, period or ascertainment method would be expected to give somewhat different proportions.
claims.uncertainty: The subgroups are small once the cohort is divided by origin and stage, which the lesson makes the learner compute: roughly 37 maternal meiosis II cases. The stage assignment depends on the centromeric-marker method and inherits that method's assumptions. Nothing in this claim describes or applies to any individual.

claims.statement: A study of 218 human oocytes from donors aged 9 to 43 distinguished three error patterns at meiosis I: meiosis I non-disjunction, the gain or loss of a whole chromosome; precocious separation of sister chromatids, in which the sister chromatids of one homolog separate already at meiosis I; and reverse segregation, in which both homologous chromosomes split their two sister chromatids already at meiosis I.
claims.scope: Human oocytes from two donor cohorts in one study, one of small antral follicles from girls and women before chemotherapy and one of oocytes from women in fertility treatment. Used by the lesson only to establish that patterns exist in which sister chromatids separate at meiosis I, which the lesson's simplified two-case model does not contain.
claims.uncertainty: The study does not state that these patterns are misclassified as meiosis II errors by conventional centromere-marker studies, and this run checked the source specifically for that statement and did not find it, so no such claim is made. The cohorts are not a general population sample.

claims.statement: Trisomic and monosomic embryos account for at least 10 per cent of human pregnancies, and for women nearing the end of their reproductive lifespan the incidence may exceed 50 per cent; approximately 0.3 per cent of newborn infants and approximately 35 per cent of spontaneous abortions are trisomic or monosomic.
claims.scope: Population-level frequencies collected in a review of human aneuploidy. These are aggregate figures across studied populations and describe no individual and no individual's probability of any outcome.
claims.uncertainty: The review presents these as approximate levels drawn from a body of literature with varying ascertainment, and gives the conception-stage figure as a range of at least 10 to 40 per cent. The may-exceed-50-per-cent figure is an upper part of a range for a specific group rather than a central estimate. Nothing here is a screening figure or a risk statement for any person.

claims.statement: In the same population-based study of trisomy 21, comparing women aged 40 and over with women under 25, the odds ratio was 5.2 for errors at maternal meiosis I and 51.4 for errors at maternal meiosis II; the authors concluded that the results support an association between advanced maternal age and errors at both divisions, that the association with meiosis I does not pinpoint the timing of the error, and that the association with meiosis II implies at least one maternal-age-related mechanism acting around the time of conception.
claims.scope: One retrospective, population-based cohort of 170 trisomy 21 cases. The design establishes an association between age band and inferred meiotic stage; it does not observe a meiosis and does not identify a mechanism. The authors' third statement is explicitly an implication they draw, not a measured finding.
claims.uncertainty: The meiosis II odds ratio rests on roughly 37 cases once the cohort is divided by origin and stage, so the point estimate is imprecise however large it is; the lesson makes the learner derive that number rather than presenting the ratio unqualified. Confidence is recorded as medium for that reason. This claim is not a risk figure for any individual and carries no screening or reproductive implication.

claims.statement: The maternal age curve for the incidence of trisomies among naturally occurring pregnancies is J-shaped, with a slight increase at the youngest maternal ages and an exponential increase in the decade preceding menopause; the presence of maternal age effects at both extremes of reproductive life, together with the age curves being variable for individual human chromosomes, points towards multiple mechanisms by which ageing affects chromosome segregation, and the genesis of human aneuploidy is described as a multi-step process caused by errors at several distinct stages of oogenesis and exacerbated by a lack of efficient checkpoints.
claims.scope: The reviewing authors' synthesis of the human aneuploidy literature as of 2012, reported here as their assessment of the state of the question rather than as a mechanism.
claims.uncertainty: This is a review's interpretation of a curve's shape and of between-chromosome variation, and interpretations of that kind are revisable. The lesson uses it to establish that no single mechanism accounts for the whole curve, which is the authors' stated position, and does not convert it into a mechanism of its own.

claims.statement: Aneuploidy in human eggs follows a U-shaped relation with female age; within that relation precocious separation of sister chromatids increased linearly with age while meiosis I non-disjunction decreased with age and reverse segregation increased in the oldest group; the study's authors propose that cohesion weakening acts as a molecular clock limiting reproductive capacity, while stating that a separate and currently unclear mechanism causes the elevated rates of meiosis I non-disjunction in young females; and a review of the same literature concludes that loss of cohesin seems unlikely to be the only force driving the increase in non-disjunction in the decade preceding menopause.
claims.scope: The state of the mechanistic question for the maternal age effect, assembled from one 2019 oocyte study and one 2012 review. The cohesion-weakening account is recorded as those authors' proposal and not as an established causal mechanism.
claims.uncertainty: This is deliberately a claim about an unsettled question. The molecular-clock account is a proposal supported by a correlation between centromeric cohesion loss and one error class in one study of 218 oocytes; the reviewing authors of a separate paper judge cohesin loss insufficient as a sole explanation; and the mechanism for the young-age arm of the curve is stated by the study's own authors to be unclear. No assessment item in this lesson keys cohesion weakening as the cause of the maternal age effect, and the lesson must not be read as endorsing it as settled.

claims.statement: Failure to recombine and suboptimally located crossovers were identified as prominent contributors to human trisomy, and over 10 per cent of all human oocytes contain at least one crossover-less bivalent; in the male almost all chromosomes are joined by at least one crossover, which does not apply to the female.
claims.scope: Human oocytes, as summarised in a review of human aneuploidy drawing on studies from the 1990s onward.
claims.uncertainty: The over-10-per-cent figure is a summary estimate in a review rather than a single measurement, and it does not sit comfortably with what compounding a separate study's per-bivalent figure of 2.60 per cent across 23 bivalents would give. The lesson reports both published figures, records the discrepancy as unresolved, and does not compute either into a further conclusion.

claims.statement: The risk of cancer is correlated with tissues that require a large amount of stem-cell divisions to maintain homeostasis, because of the additional risk of random mutation accumulation.
claims.scope: A correlational statement across tissues, reported in a review of the colonic crypt, used here only to connect the crypt's division load to the subject of lesson 10 of this block.
claims.uncertainty: This is a correlation across tissue types reported in review prose, not a causal claim about any tissue and not a risk statement about any person. The lesson does not develop it; cell death, senescence and cancer are the subject of PREM-05.10.

terms.definition: The division that produces gametes: one round of DNA replication followed by two cell divisions, so that a diploid cell gives rise to haploid products. Its first division separates the members of each homologous pair from each other and its second separates sister chromatids, and it happens only in the germ line. A somatic tissue such as the colonic crypt never performs it.

The two versions of one chromosome that a person carries, one inherited from each parent. They are very similar in DNA sequence without being identical. The two are partners rather than copies of each other, and that distinction carries most of this lesson: partners are separated at the first meiotic division, copies at the second.

One of the strands of a chromosome that has been replicated. A chromosome that has just been copied consists of two chromatids joined at the centromere and still counts as one chromosome, so a cell can hold 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids at the same time. Keeping the two counts apart is the commonest difficulty in this material.

The two identical chromatids produced when one chromosome is replicated, joined at the centromere. Because one was copied from the other they carry the same DNA sequence, which is what distinguishes them from the two homologs of a pair. An ordinary mitotic division separates sister chromatids; meiosis separates them only at its second division.

The constricted region of a chromosome at which its sister chromatids are joined and at which the spindle takes hold to move it. In this lesson the centromere also carries information: a reciprocal exchange between homologs swaps the material beyond the point of exchange, so each chromatid keeps its own centromere, and the parental origin of a centromere is therefore what independent assortment sorts and what a marker can be read back from.

The structure formed when a replicated chromosome pairs with its replicated homolog during meiosis. A bivalent contains four chromatids: two sister chromatids from each of the two homologs. Some texts call the same four-chromatid structure a tetrad; this lesson uses bivalent throughout.

Holding both members of every homologous pair. A diploid human cell carries 46 chromosomes as 23 pairs. Ploidy counts chromosomes and not copies of DNA, so a cell whose chromosomes have just been replicated is still diploid even though it then holds two DNA copies of each chromosome. Somatic cells are diploid and stay diploid through every division they make.

Holding one member of every homologous pair. A haploid human cell carries 23 chromosomes. Because ploidy counts chromosomes rather than DNA copies, a cell can be haploid and still hold two copies of each chromosome's DNA: that is exactly the state after the first meiotic division, and it is why a second division is needed before the cell is a gamete.

A haploid cell whose function is to fuse with another gamete. In humans the two kinds are the sperm cell and the egg cell. Gametes are the only cells meiosis produces, and producing them is the only job meiosis does.

The single diploid cell formed when two gametes fuse. Every cell of the resulting body descends from it by ordinary division, which is why a chromosome error present in the zygote is present everywhere while one arising later is confined to a patch.
The lineage of cells that leads to gametes. It is the only lineage in which meiosis occurs. Novelty is the germ line's product: new combinations of chromosomes are what it exists to generate.

Any cell of the body that is not on the path to becoming a gamete. Somatic cells divide mitotically, remain diploid, and never undergo meiosis. Every cell in a colonic crypt is somatic, which is why genetic novelty there is damage rather than product.

The apparatus of protein fibres a dividing cell builds to move its chromosomes. It has two ends, called poles, and pulls each chromosome toward one pole or the other. Because one spindle has two poles, one division yields two cells, and that limit is the reason meiosis needs two divisions to reach four products.

The stage of a cell division at which the spindle actually pulls and the chromosomes move apart. Meiosis has two of them: at anaphase I the homologs separate, and at anaphase II the sister chromatids separate.

The rule that which member of one homologous pair goes to a given pole at the first meiotic division is settled independently of every other pair. With 23 pairs it gives a binary choice repeated 23 times, so 2 to the 23, about 8.4 million, distinct patterns of parental origin across the 23 centromeres. That count is exact for what it counts and ignores crossing over entirely.

The process in which meiosis deliberately breaks its own DNA and repairs each break using the homolog as the template. Most breaks are repaired without any exchange of arms; where the repair does produce a reciprocal exchange, the outcome is crossing over. Where this lesson writes recombination without qualification it means this meiotic process; the bare word is broader in general use and covers other kinds of DNA exchange that this lesson does not treat.

The reciprocal exchange of segments between two homologs during meiosis, so that beyond the point of exchange the DNA of one homolog's chromatid runs continuously into what was the other's. It does two jobs at once: it makes new combinations within a chromosome, and it physically ties the pair together so that the first division has something to pull against.

One completed reciprocal exchange between homologs, and so one countable event of crossing over. Crossovers are counted per meiotic cell by staining for a protein that gathers at them: measured means are about 49 per cell in human males and about 69 in human females, roughly two and three per chromosome pair. A crossover is a single event, whereas crossing over is the process that produces it.

The physical connection between two homologs produced by a crossover, and the thing that holds the pair together until the first anaphase separates them. A bivalent with no chiasma has nothing holding it, which is why an absence of crossing over leads to chromosomes being missegregated. The plural is chiasmata.

The protein glue holding sister chromatids together, running along the chromatid arms and also through the centromere. It is one substance in two locations, released in two stages: the arm cohesion at the start of anaphase I, and the centromeric cohesion only at the second division. That staging fixes the order of the two separations, and because the swapped arms beyond a crossover are held by arm cohesion, cutting it is also what lets the chiasma give way. This lesson shortens the name to cohesion where the context is chromosomes; it is unrelated to the cell-to-cell adhesion PREM-BIO-007 treats.

A reductional division reduces the number of chromosomes per cell; an equational division does not. Meiosis I is reductional because it separates the two homologs of each pair, taking a cell from 46 chromosomes to 23. Meiosis II is equational because it separates sister chromatids, which lowers the chromatid count while leaving the chromosome count at 23. An ordinary mitotic division is equational in the same sense.

The failure of chromosomes to separate normally during a division, leaving one product with an extra copy and another with none. In meiosis it can happen at either division, and the two cases leave different signatures: a failure at the first division yields products carrying two different homologs, and a failure at the second yields a product carrying two copies of one homolog.

A description of one position on a chromosome, comparing the copies a cell holds there. If the copies read differently in DNA sequence, the cell is heterozygous at that position; if they read the same, it is homozygous. The words describe the comparison at that position and nothing more, saying nothing about a whole chromosome and nothing about any trait. This lesson uses them only at the centromere, where they distinguish two copies that are different homologs from two copies of one homolog.

An unbalanced chromosome number, in which certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs. A balanced number is euploid. Aneuploidy can arise from a meiotic non-disjunction before an individual exists, or from a mitotic error afterwards, and telling those apart is a question about when rather than about the chromosomes themselves.

Trisomy is a diploid genome that has gained one chromosome, written 2N+1; monosomy is one that has lost a chromosome, written 2N-1. A gamete carrying two copies of a chromosome gives a trisomy on fusing with a normal gamete, and one carrying none gives a monosomy. Both are whole-chromosome changes, as distinct from segmental changes in which only pieces of chromosomes are gained or lost.

The small cell discarded at each of the two asymmetric divisions of oogenesis. Half the genome is segregated into the polar bodies, which is why one meiosis in the female yields a single functional gamete instead of four. The source this lesson follows describes two polar bodies, one per division; accounts giving three exist and the lesson records that disagreement rather than settling it.

Oogenesis is the production of egg cells in the ovary; spermatogenesis is the production of sperm cells in the testis. Both run meiosis and they run it differently: spermatogenesis divides symmetrically to four functional gametes and continues throughout life, while oogenesis divides asymmetrically to one functional gamete, begins before birth, and arrests in the first division for decades.

A cell with the capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny. The definition is about capacity rather than continuous activity: some stem-cell populations are quiescent until activated, while others cycle actively. In this lesson the term names the 12 to 16 cells at the base of a colonic crypt whose divisions renew the lining, and every one of those divisions is somatic.

alignment.note: PREM-BIO-001 defines stem cell for this course and this lesson keeps that meaning without alteration: capacity to self-renew and to produce differentiated progeny, with capacity distinguished from continuous division. Nothing is narrowed or extended, and the definition is not converted into an activity-based one even though this lesson quotes a division interval for the crypt population. PREM-BIO-006 adopted the same sense earlier. What this lesson adds is only that these divisions are somatic and so never meiotic.

  1. One claim is an inference, not a sourced mechanism. claim-chiasma-resolution-reading holds that releasing arm cohesion is what allows a chiasma to stop holding a pair. It is this lesson's reading of two statements that sit adjacent in one textbook chapter, its support is recorded as inference, its confidence as medium, and scene 2 tells the learner in prose that it is a reading rather than a quotation. It is the first thing to challenge.
  2. An unresolved discrepancy is reported rather than settled. A per-bivalent frequency of 2.60 per cent of female bivalents lacking a crossover marker, compounded across 23 bivalents under an independence assumption, gives about 45 per cent of oocytes carrying at least one such bivalent, against a review's figure of over 10 per cent. Scene 6 states both published figures, gives three candidate explanations, declines to choose, and marks the 45 per cent as what an independence assumption yields rather than a measured quantity. No assessment item depends on it.

  1. The central "why two divisions" argument is the lesson's own reasoning, not a sourced one. Scene 2 argues that meiosis performs two different halvings: the chromosome number at division I and the number of DNA copies per chromosome at division II, and that a cell haploid by chromosome count is still not a gamete because each of its 23 chromosomes holds two DNA copies. Every component fact is sourced, but the argument assembling them is the lesson's construction and no cited source presents it in this form. A reviewer should check it on the biology rather than on the citations.

    Recorded for the reviewer's benefit: an earlier proposed version of this argument held that two such cells fusing would give a zygote whose first division hands each daughter 23 chromosomes, so the body would be haploid. That version is wrong, and it was not used. The zygote's first division is mitotic and separates sister chromatids, so each daughter would receive one chromatid from each of the 46 chromosomes and would be diploid. The argument the lesson actually makes rests on DNA copy number and on each parent contributing one copy rather than two.
